SECTION I
L	In my childhood, fire had two faces. The first: friendly, vivacious, exuberant. Like a puppy
with sharp teeth and too much energy, capable of doing damage but not out of malicious
intent. Fire as community, as celebration, as connection. Beach bonfires made of sand-crusted
driftwood, pulsing an unpredictable pattern of light and heat into the starry night, sending
glimmers off the black lake. Pine-scented fires made from dried-out Christmas trees, around
which my cousins and aunts and uncles and friends huddled, the flames sometimes erupting
blue as a forgotten strand of tinsel burned up, nearby ice hissing as it melted. Campfires to
cook hot dogs, roast vegetables wrapped in foil or toast marshmallows to the perfect shade of
golden brown. Simmering prairie burns that leave the earth blackened, amplifying the sun-fed
warmth to spring plants, smelling like sweet charcoal. I loved all the fires, always volunteered
to get them started, wanted nothing more than to sit and watch the ripple and dance of flame
till there was nothing but snapping embers.
The second: deadly, unpredictable, bad to know. House fires that killed sleeping children or
leveled historic cities. Grease fires in the kitchen, subverting the normal knowledge of
quenching them with water. Frayed wires allowing electrons to escape their confines and
ignite furniture. Stop, drop and roll; in emergencies break glass; test the smoke detector on a
regular basis. If that alarm goes off, feel the doorknob before opening your bedroom door.
Block smoke with a towel. Open the window, hang from the ledge and drop if you have no
other option; better to break an ankle than burn to death or die of smoke inhalation. Fire has
no place indoors, except on carefully monitored candles, and the friendliness of a bonfire
should not be mistaken for house-training.
Wildfires belong to this second category as well, but on a far more massive scale. They were
also, notably, not a threat to my particular corner of North America; the Chicago fire of 1871
was old history by the time I moved there, even if it is represented on the city’s flag in the
form of a star. We had heat waves and polar vortexes, blizzards and tornadoes, floods and
droughts. I took comfort in the knowledge that fire happened in different ecological regimes.

content.passageText:
IL.	The idea of human existence as the continuous journey of a singular self is not just typical of
European life-writing but a convention of Western literature and culture as such. In
philosophy, it is what we see conceptualised in essentialist and narrative accounts of selfhood,
which maintain that some form of persisting personal essence and sense of narrative
coherence is not only natural for humans, but necessary for acting morally and living a
meaningful life.
Living without a sense of self or narrative identity as I do in a culture of strong selves and big
narratives is in many ways exciting. My self-experience of insubstantiality and emptiness
seems to come with a certain existential flexibility and freedom, and specifically, a
susceptibility to absorption in other people’s stories. Having little or no sense of an inner
essence, and only a vague feeling of boundaries between myself and what is around me, I find
it easy to immerse myself in narrative fiction as well as the real lives of others. This might

explain why the line between fiction and reality has been diffuse in my life. Most of my
romantic relationships have been with professional storytellers — writers, journalists,
filmmakers — working creatively with self-representation. I’ve become entangled in other
people’s narrative experiments, and appeared as a character in published life-stories several
times. This has given me rich and deep experiences of immersion in other worlds and of
merging with other minds. But I’ve also always felt divergent, un-mirrored by the narratives
of human existence I’ve been submerged in. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Literature does not just passively reflect our intuitions and ideas. It shapes our expectations
and conceptions, influences our perception and experience of ourselves and the world. It
shapes and manifests our shared experience as a culture. It has confused me that my own
experience didn’t match what I read about in books or encountered in the culture around me.
I’ve even been clinically assessed for borderline personality disorder — symptoms of which
include inner emptiness, an unstable sense of identity, and dissociation. [Word Count: 336]

content.passageText:
Ill.	At a moment when the world once again teeters on the edge of catastrophic conflict, I find
myself returning to the memory of another time in the 1960s, when dissent was not only
possible but transformative. Today, as war rhetoric escalates, and the language of power
grows increasingly unrestrained, I am struck by the absence of a comparable collective moral
force.
I came of age in the mid-1960s, entering my undergraduate years at a time when the world
seemed alive with argument, possibility, and resistance. Unlike the present, the university
was a space charged with debate and intellectual exchange. We did not simply inherit the
world, we interrogated it.
But just as formative as the university were the informal spaces we inhabited. The coffeehouse
culture of those years, the dimly lit rooms filled with cigarette smoke, the clattering cups, and
restless voices, became an extension of intellectual life. It was there that ideas found their
urgency. Conversations moved from literature to politics, from philosophy to the daily
headlines of war and protest. Democracy, freedom, human rights far from being abstract
concepts, were debated intensely, often passionately.
Music, theatre, and radical thought became some of the most powerful carriers of this spirit of
interrogation. Sitting with friends, often late into the night, we read the incendiary writings of
Jean-Paul Sartre and Herbert Marcuse, whose critiques of consumer capitalism and
conformity unsettled our certainties. Their insistence that modern societies could produce not
freedom but new forms of domination forced us to rethink the very meaning of democracy. At
the same time, the political courage of figures like Martin Luther King Jr., with his
uncompromising stand against racial injustice, and Malcolm X, with his fierce articulation of
dignity and resistance, expanded our sense of what dissent could achieve. These were not
distant figures; they were intellectual and moral presences that shaped our conversations,

compelling us to confront power, inequality, and the ethical responsibilities of citizenship.
[Word Count: 322]

page/when-resistance-became-memory /article70857854.ece

content.passageText:
IV.	A US jury on Wednesday found Meta and YouTube guilty of deliberately designing addictive
products that caused harm to a young user in a landmark social media addiction trial that will
likely serve as a bellwether for future cases. The jurors in a Los Angeles court found the tech
companies to be negligent in the design of the platform and in failing to warn users of its
dangers. The jury said yes to questions that asked whether the platforms acted with malice,
oppression and fraud. The jury awarded damages of $6 million, with Meta bearing around 70%
of the liability and YouTube the remaining 30%.
Meta owns Facebook and Instagram and has over 3.5 billion users, while nine out of ten
American teenagers aged 13-17 overwhelmingly use YouTube, according to a 2025 Pew
Research Center report. Meta has long been accused of addictive platform design by parents,
child safety groups and tech policy advocates, and of causing mental health issues resulting in
eating disorders and self-harm. The present case is the first in a flurry of lawsuits filed by
teenagers, school districts and states, claiming that platforms like Meta-owned Instagram and
‘YouTube were designed to encourage excessive use by millions of young Americans. Twenty-
year-old KGM started using YouTube when she was six, and Instagram at nine. She claimed
that her addiction to social media led to anxiety, depression and body dysmorphia. The
plaintiffs have argued that social media should be identified as a product and thus its design
and other components must be held to product liability standards.
Mark Lanier, her lawyer, compared this design to dopamine-seeking “slot machines”, and said
that YouTube and Meta were operating like “digital casinos” with their endless scroll features
fuelling dopamine hits and thus, addiction. Past lawsuits against social media companies over
the harm they cause frequently ran into Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act 1996,
which says that internet platforms cannot be held liable for content posted by their users.
Courts had read it broadly enough to kill most lawsuits before they got anywhere near a jury.
The plaintiffs in this case avoided that barrier by changing the claim itself, framing it instead
around product design. It thus drew on principles from product liability law, where liability
can arise from how a product is built rather than what it contains. [Word Count: 319]

youtube-lost-us-design-liability-case-10602733/

IV.	A US jury on Wednesday found Meta and YouTube guilty of deliberately designing addictive
products that caused harm to a young user in a landmark social media addiction trial that will
likely serve as a bellwether for future cases. The jurors in a Los Angeles court found the tech
companies to be negligent in the design of the platform and in failing to warn users of its
dangers. The jury said yes to questions that asked whether the platforms acted with malice,
oppression and fraud. The jury awarded damages of $6 million, with Meta bearing around 70%
of the liability and YouTube the remaining 30%.
Meta owns Facebook and Instagram and has over 3.5 billion users, while nine out of ten
American teenagers aged 13-17 overwhelmingly use YouTube, according to a 2025 Pew
Research Center report. Meta has long been accused of addictive platform design by parents,
child safety groups and tech policy advocates, and of causing mental health issues resulting in
eating disorders and self-harm. The present case is the first in a flurry of lawsuits filed by
teenagers, school districts and states, claiming that platforms like Meta-owned Instagram and
‘YouTube were designed to encourage excessive use by millions of young Americans. Twenty-
year-old KGM started using YouTube when she was six, and Instagram at nine. She claimed
that her addiction to social media led to anxiety, depression and body dysmorphia. The
plaintiffs have argued that social media should be identified as a product and thus its design
and other components must be held to product liability standards.
Mark Lanier, her lawyer, compared this design to dopamine-seeking “slot machines”, and said
that YouTube and Meta were operating like “digital casinos” with their endless scroll features
fuelling dopamine hits and thus, addiction. Past lawsuits against social media companies over
the harm they cause frequently ran into Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act 1996,
which says that internet platforms cannot be held liable for content posted by their users.
Courts had read it broadly enough to kill most lawsuits before they got anywhere near a jury.
The plaintiffs in this case avoided that barrier by changing the claim itself, framing it instead
around product design. It thus drew on principles from product liability law, where liability
can arise from how a product is built rather than what it contains. [Word Count: 319]

VIII. India and the five Nordic nations—Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden—met in
Oslo on 19 May 2026 for the Third India-Nordic Summit. The summit marked a significant
evolution in relations, as both sides elevated their engagement to a Green Technology and
Innovation Strategic Partnership. The partnership seeks to strengthen cooperation in
sustainable development, renewable energy, digital infrastructure, climate action, innovation,
and emerging technologies. www.lawpreptutorial.com
A major economic outcome of the summit was the endorsement of the operationalisation of the
India-EFTA Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA) and the conclusion of the
India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA) negotiations. Under TEPA, EFTA
countries aim to facilitate investments worth USD 100 billion in India and contribute to the
creation of one million direct jobs. Leaders also emphasised the importance of diversifying
supply chains and improving connectivity between Europe and the Indo-Pacific through
initiatives such as the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC).
The summit further highlighted cooperation in artificial intelligence, 5G and 6G technologies,
maritime security, climate finance, green hydrogen, and critical minerals. Nordic leaders
welcomed India's role as an observer in the Arctic Council and supported deeper collaboration

in Arctic research, especially concerning climate change and its implications for monsoon
systems.
On strategic matters, the Nordic countries reiterated support for India's aspiration for
permanent membership of a reformed United Nations Security Council and welcomed its
application to the Nuclear Suppliers Group. The summit also underscored the shared
commitment of both sides to a rules-based international order, sustainable development, and
international law. The next India-Nordic Summit is scheduled to be hosted by Finland.

IX.	The year 2026 marks the 500th anniversary of the First Battle of Panipat, one of the most
consequential battles in Indian history. Fought on 21 April 1526 between Zahir-ud-din
Muhammad Babur and Sultan Ibrahim Lodi of the Delhi Sultanate, the battle fundamentally
altered the political landscape of North India. Babur, a Timurid ruler from Central Asia, had
long sought to establish a stable kingdom after losing and regaining territories in the region of
Transoxiana and Kabul.
The battle is particularly significant because it demonstrated the effectiveness of new military
technologies and tactics. Babur employed field artillery, matchlock firearms, and the Ottoman-
inspired tulughma and araba systems, enabling his numerically smaller army to overcome the
much larger forces of Ibrahim Lodi. The defeat and death of Ibrahim Lodi brought an end to
the Lodi dynasty and substantially weakened the Delhi Sultanate.
Historians often regard the battle not merely as a military victory but as the beginning of a
new imperial order. The success at Panipat laid the foundation for the Mughal Empire, which
would eventually become one of the most influential empires in South Asian history. However,
Babur’s position was not immediately secure; he subsequently faced challenges from Rajput
forces under Rana Sanga and Afghan chiefs seeking to restore their influence.
The battle also highlights a recurring theme in history: technological innovation and strategic
adaptation can sometimes outweigh numerical superiority. Consequently, the First Battle of
Panipat remains a key event for understanding the transition from the late medieval to the
early modern period in the Indian subcontinent.
Source: 500 Years of Mughals: How Babur Won First Battle of Panipat in 1526

IX.	The year 2026 marks the 500th anniversary of the First Battle of Panipat, one of the most
consequential battles in Indian history. Fought on 21 April 1526 between Zahir-ud-din
Muhammad Babur and Sultan Ibrahim Lodi of the Delhi Sultanate, the battle fundamentally
altered the political landscape of North India. Babur, a Timurid ruler from Central Asia, had
long sought to establish a stable kingdom after losing and regaining territories in the region of
Transoxiana and Kabul.
The battle is particularly significant because it demonstrated the effectiveness of new military
technologies and tactics. Babur employed field artillery, matchlock firearms, and the Ottoman-
inspired tulughma and araba systems, enabling his numerically smaller army to overcome the
much larger forces of Ibrahim Lodi. The defeat and death of Ibrahim Lodi brought an end to
the Lodi dynasty and substantially weakened the Delhi Sultanate.
Historians often regard the battle not merely as a military victory but as the beginning of a
new imperial order. The success at Panipat laid the foundation for the Mughal Empire, which
would eventually become one of the most influential empires in South Asian history. However,
Babur’s position was not immediately secure; he subsequently faced challenges from Rajput
forces under Rana Sanga and Afghan chiefs seeking to restore their influence.
The battle also highlights a recurring theme in history: technological innovation and strategic
adaptation can sometimes outweigh numerical superiority. Consequently, the First Battle of
Panipat remains a key event for understanding the transition from the late medieval to the
early modern period in the Indian subcontinent.

SECTION III
X.	Administrative tribunals are quasi-judicial institutions created by statute to adjudicate
disputes relating to administrative matters. They are not regular courts, but they exercise
judicial and quasi-judicial powers in specific areas assigned by law, such as recruitment,
appointment, promotion, transfer, disciplinary proceedings, pension, retirement benefits,
taxation, labour matters and other specialised subjects. Their proceedings are treated as
judicial proceedings, and they possess powers similar to civil courts, including summoning
witnesses, receiving evidence, administering oaths, reviewing decisions and deciding matters
ex parte. Their main purpose is to ensure speedy justice, review administrative decisions,
resolve service disputes and reduce pendency before ordinary courts.
The growth of tribunalisation in India began before independence with bodies like the Income
Tax Appellate Tribunal. After independence, the expanding role of the State and increasing
administrative disputes made specialised adjudicatory bodies necessary. On _ the
recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act,
1976 inserted Part XIV-A into the Constitution, containing Articles 323A and 323B. Article
323A empowers Parliament to create administrative tribunals for disputes relating to
recruitment and conditions of service of public servants under the Union, States, local
authorities, public corporations and government-controlled bodies. Article 323B enables
Parliament and State Legislatures to create tribunals for specialised matters such as taxation,
foreign exchange, industrial disputes, land reforms, elections, rent and essential commodities.
Administrative tribunals have statutory origin, quasi-judicial nature, limited jurisdiction,
subject expertise and flexible procedure. They are not strictly bound by the Code of Civil
Procedure or the Indian Evidence Act, but they must follow principles of natural justice,
including fair hearing, absence of bias and reasoned decisions. Unlike ordinary courts, which
possess general jurisdiction and are part of the traditional judicial system, tribunals are
specialised bodies and may include administrative or technical experts.
The Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 was enacted under Article 823A and provides for the
Central Administrative Tribunal, State Administrative Tribunals and Joint Administrative
Tribunals. The Central Administrative Tribunal deals with service matters of Central
Government employees, civilian defence employees, members of All India Services and
employees of government-controlled authorities, excluding armed forces personnel, Supreme
Court and High Court staff, and parliamentary secretariat staff.
In S.P. Sampath Kumar v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld the validity of tribunals
as effective alternative mechanisms, while recognising judicial review as part of the basic
structure. In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, the Court held that tribunals are courts of
first instance, but their decisions remain subject to scrutiny by High Courts under Articles 226
and 227. Administrative tribunals provide speedy, expert and inexpensive justice, but

concerns remain regarding independence, uniform procedure, administrative control and
reappointment. Recent tribunal reforms and proposals for a National Tribunal Commission
aim to strengthen independence and uniformity in tribunal administration. [Word Count: 454]

disputes relating to administrative matters. They are not regular courts, but they exercise

appointment, promotion, transfer, disciplinary proceedings, pension, retirement benefits,
taxation, labour matters and other specialised subjects. Their proceedings are treated as
judicial proceedings, and they possess powers similar to civil courts, including summoning
witnesses, receiving evidence, administering oaths, reviewing decisions and deciding matters
ex parte. Their main purpose is to ensure speedy justice, review administrative decisions,
resolve service disputes and reduce pendency before ordinary courts.
The growth of tribunalisation in India began before independence with bodies like the Income
Tax Appellate Tribunal. After independence, the expanding role of the State and increasing
administrative disputes made specialised adjudicatory bodies necessary. On _ the
recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act,
1976 inserted Part XIV-A into the Constitution, containing Articles 323A and 323B. Article

recruitment and conditions of service of public servants under the Union, States, local
authorities, public corporations and government-controlled bodies. Article 323B enables
Parliament and State Legislatures to create tribunals for specialised matters such as taxation,
foreign exchange, industrial disputes, land reforms, elections, rent and essential commodities.
Administrative tribunals have statutory origin, quasi-judicial nature, limited jurisdiction,
subject expertise and flexible procedure. They are not strictly bound by the Code of Civil
Procedure or the Indian Evidence Act, but they must follow principles of natural justice,
including fair hearing, absence of bias and reasoned decisions. Unlike ordinary courts, which
possess general jurisdiction and are part of the traditional judicial system, tribunals are
specialised bodies and may include administrative or technical experts.

Central Administrative Tribunal, State Administrative Tribunals and Joint Administrative
Tribunals. The Central Administrative Tribunal deals with service matters of Central
Government employees, civilian defence employees, members of All India Services and
employees of government-controlled authorities, excluding armed forces personnel, Supreme
Court and High Court staff, and parliamentary secretariat staff.

as effective alternative mechanisms, while recognising judicial review as part of the basic
structure. In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, the Court held that tribunals are courts of
first instance, but their decisions remain subject to scrutiny by High Courts under Articles 226
and 227. Administrative tribunals provide speedy, expert and inexpensive justice, but

concerns remain regarding independence, uniform procedure, administrative control and

content.passageText:
XI.	An agreement is a mutual understanding or arrangement between two or more parties. It
represents the meeting of minds where each party agrees to do or not do something.
Agreements can be oral, written, formal, informal, or implied by conduct. Section 2(e) of the
Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines an agreement as “every promise and every set of promises,
forming the consideration for each other.” In simple terms, when one person makes an offer
and the other accepts it, it becomes an agreement. Agreements are flexible in nature and may
be verbal, written, or implied by actions. However, not all agreements are enforceable by law.
For example, a verbal promise between friends to meet, an informal arrangement to share
expenses, or an email exchange regarding meeting details may be agreements, but they may
not create legal consequences.
A contract, on the other hand, is a legally binding agreement that the law recognises and
enforces. Section 2(h) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines a contract as “an agreement
enforceable by law.” A contract creates legal rights and obligations between the parties. If one
party fails to perform their part, the other party may seek legal remedies such as
compensation, specific performance, or cancellation. Examples of contracts include
employment contracts, lease agreements, sale deeds, service agreements and loan agreements.
Thus, every contract is an agreement, but every agreement is not a contract.
For an agreement to become a contract, it must satisfy certain essential elements. There must
be a lawful offer by one party and an unequivocal acceptance by the other. There must be
lawful consideration, meaning something of value such as money, goods, services, or a promise
to do or not do something. The parties must be competent to contract, meaning they must be
major, of sound mind, and not disqualified by law. Their consent must be free and genuine, not
caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake. The object must be
lawful, and the terms must be certain and capable of performance. If any of these essential
elements are absent, the agreement remains unenforceable.www.lawpreptutorial.com
The main difference between agreement and contract lies in legal enforceability. An
agreement is a wider term and may or may not create legal obligations, whereas a contract is a
narrower term and always creates enforceable rights and duties. Agreements may be informal
and may lack consideration, but contracts generally require lawful consideration, free consent,

lawful object and certainty. A simple promise to lend a bicycle may be an agreement, but a
written sale of the bicycle for 75,000 is a contract. Therefore, agreements are suitable for
informal arrangements, while contracts are necessary for transactions involving value,
duration, legal protection and remedies. [Word Count: 449]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from: https://lawbhoomi.com/differences-between-
agreement-and-contract/

content.passageText:
XII. Peaceful settlement of disputes in international law, also known as pacific settlement of
international disputes, is a fundamental principle requiring States to resolve their
disagreements by peaceful means so that international peace, security and justice are not
endangered. Its origin can be traced to the Hague Peace Conferences of 1899 and 1907, which
produced conventions for the pacific settlement of disputes. The principle gained greater
importance after the prohibition on the use of force under Article 2(4) of the UN Charter.
Article 2(3) of the UN Charter provides that all members shall settle their international
disputes by peaceful means. This obligation was reaffirmed in the 1982 Manila Declaration on
the Peaceful Settlement of International Disputes.
An international dispute may be understood as a disagreement involving at least one State
and another State, international organisation, natural person, legal person, institution or
corporation from another part of the world. The Black’s Law Dictionary defines a dispute as a
conflict or controversy, especially one giving rise to legal proceedings. In international law,
peaceful settlement is treated as a continuous legal duty, where States participate as equal
units in rights. In Military and Paramilitary Activities in and against Nicaragua, the ICJ
recognised that parties to a dispute must seek a solution by pacific methods. However, the UN
Charter does not compel parties to adopt one fixed method. Article 33 lists peaceful methods
such as negotiation, enquiry, mediation, conciliation, arbitration, judicial settlement and
resort to regional arrangements. If parties fail to settle the dispute, Article 37 requires them to
refer the matter to the Security Council.
Negotiation is the oldest, simplest and most common method. It involves direct discussion
between disputing parties without third-party intervention. India and Sri Lanka settled their
boundary dispute through negotiation in 1974, and the Farakka Barrage issue between India
and Bangladesh was also resolved through this method. Good offices involve a third friendly
State, individual or organisation suggesting settlement without directly participating in
discussions, as seen in the Shatt-al-Arab dispute between Iran and Iraq through the President
of Algeria. Mediation involves active participation of a neutral third party who gives
suggestions and helps parties reach settlement; the Tashkent Agreement between India and
Pakistan is an example.
Conciliation refers disputes to a commission or committee which proposes a settlement,
though its recommendations are not binding. Arbitration and judicial settlement are
adjudicative methods because they result in binding decisions. Arbitration involves a chosen
arbitrator or tribunal, while judicial settlement involves courts such as the International
Court of Justice. International disputes may be legal or political, but international law mainly
deals with legal disputes. In Nicaragua v. Honduras, the Court clarified that it concerns itself
only with legal aspects of a dispute. [Word Count: 449]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from: https://blog.ipleaders.in/settlement-of-
disputes-in-international-law/

Two neighbouring States dispute responsibility for pollution in a shared lake. State X agrees
to one meeting, then refuses further discussion and says State Y must first accept X’s superior
historical status in the region. State Y insists that peaceful settlement is not a one-time
courtesy and that both States must participate as equal legal units while seeking a solution.
State X argues that stronger States may decide when talks end.
Which answer best applies?
options: State X succeeds because powerful States may end settlement efforts unilaterally.
State X succeeds because one meeting fully satisfies all peaceful settlement duties.

State Y succeeds because equality between States is irrelevant during environmental
disputes.
State Y succeeds because peaceful settlement is a continuous duty among equal States.

State M is correct because all disputes must go only to courts.
State M is correct because negotiation has no value in international law.
State N is correct because parties cannot choose between peaceful methods.

content.passageText:
XII. Peaceful settlement of disputes in international law, also known as pacific settlement of
international disputes, is a fundamental principle requiring States to resolve their
disagreements by peaceful means so that international peace, security and justice are not
endangered. Its origin can be traced to the Hague Peace Conferences of 1899 and 1907, which
produced conventions for the pacific settlement of disputes. The principle gained greater
importance after the prohibition on the use of force under Article 2(4) of the UN Charter.
Article 2(3) of the UN Charter provides that all members shall settle their international
disputes by peaceful means. This obligation was reaffirmed in the 1982 Manila Declaration on
the Peaceful Settlement of International Disputes.
An international dispute may be understood as a disagreement involving at least one State
and another State, international organisation, natural person, legal person, institution or
corporation from another part of the world. The Black’s Law Dictionary defines a dispute as a
conflict or controversy, especially one giving rise to legal proceedings. In international law,
peaceful settlement is treated as a continuous legal duty, where States participate as equal
units in rights. In Military and Paramilitary Activities in and against Nicaragua, the ICJ
recognised that parties to a dispute must seek a solution by pacific methods. However, the UN
Charter does not compel parties to adopt one fixed method. Article 33 lists peaceful methods
such as negotiation, enquiry, mediation, conciliation, arbitration, judicial settlement and
resort to regional arrangements. If parties fail to settle the dispute, Article 37 requires them to
refer the matter to the Security Council.
Negotiation is the oldest, simplest and most common method. It involves direct discussion
between disputing parties without third-party intervention. India and Sri Lanka settled their
boundary dispute through negotiation in 1974, and the Farakka Barrage issue between India
and Bangladesh was also resolved through this method. Good offices involve a third friendly
State, individual or organisation suggesting settlement without directly participating in
discussions, as seen in the Shatt-al-Arab dispute between Iran and Iraq through the President
of Algeria. Mediation involves active participation of a neutral third party who gives
suggestions and helps parties reach settlement; the Tashkent Agreement between India and
Pakistan is an example.
Conciliation refers disputes to a commission or committee which proposes a settlement,
though its recommendations are not binding. Arbitration and judicial settlement are
adjudicative methods because they result in binding decisions. Arbitration involves a chosen
arbitrator or tribunal, while judicial settlement involves courts such as the International
Court of Justice. International disputes may be legal or political, but international law mainly
deals with legal disputes. In Nicaragua v. Honduras, the Court clarified that it concerns itself
only with legal aspects of a dispute. [Word Count: 449]

disputes-in-international-law/

content.passageText:
XIII. Bailable offences are those offences where the accused has a legal right to be released on bail.
Under BNSS, such offences are specifically marked as bailable in the First Schedule. These
offences are generally treated as less serious, and therefore the accused is not required to
remain in custody till the court conducts an elaborate hearing. The primary feature of a
bailable offence is that the police officer in charge can release the accused on bail after arrest
once the required bond is furnished. There is no need to wait for a court order or a complex
hearing at this stage. These offences usually involve minor harm, limited property loss,
personal disputes, or conduct having low impact on public safety.
The classification of some offences as bailable is based on the idea that unnecessary detention
should be avoided where the alleged act does not involve grave injury, severe consequences,
major threat to public order, or serious social harm. Common examples include simple hurt,
minor trespass, rash or negligent driving, obstruction in public pathways, defamation,
criminal intimidation, minor cheating, mischief causing small loss, falsification of accounts,
negligent acts likely to spread infection, and misconduct in public by intoxicated persons.
Although bailable offences are generally minor, an offence with higher punishment may
sometimes still be classified as bailable due to legislative intent or specific policy
considerations.
Non-bailable offences are more serious offences where the accused does not have a right to
bail. Release from custody depends on the discretion of the court. These offences often involve
serious violence, sexual offences, crimes against children, repeated criminal conduct, major
financial fraud, threat to national security, or significant danger to public order. In such cases,
the court examines the gravity of allegations, the nature of evidence, possibility of the accused
fleeing, past criminal record, risk of influencing witnesses, impact on society or victim, and the
need for proper investigation before granting bail.
The major difference between bailable and non-bailable offences lies in the right to bail and
the authority granting it. In bailable offences, bail is available as a matter of right and may be
granted by the police officer or the court. In non-bailable offences, bail is not a right and only

the court can grant it after judicial scrutiny. Bailable offences involve lower punishment and
limited threat, while non-bailable offences carry higher penalties and serious social impact.
Examples of non-bailable offences include waging war against the Government, counterfeiting
currency, murder, dowry death, abetment of suicide, attempt to murder, trafficking, rape,
robbery, dacoity, serious criminal breach of trust, major cheating, and cruelty against married
women. Courts may also impose conditions such as travel restrictions, regular police
reporting, or surrender of passport while granting bail in non-bailable cases.
[Word Count: 453]

XIV. In tort law, when a wrongful act is committed by more than one person, the persons involved
may be joint tortfeasors or independent tortfeasors. Joint tortfeasors are those who act
together or in furtherance of a common design, resulting in damage to another person. Their
liability is joint and several, which means that each tortfeasor is individually liable for the
entire damage and also collectively liable with the others. Independent tortfeasors, on the
other hand, act separately and without coordination. Even if their separate acts cause the
same injury, their liability arises from separate causes of action. In The Koursk, it was
observed that joint liability requires concerted action towards a common end, and mere
similarity of conduct is not enough.
The difference between independent and joint tortfeasors is important for determining
remedies. In Thompson v. London County Council, damage occurred due to separate negligent
acts of different parties, and the Court held that they were not joint tortfeasors because their

Which conclusion is strongest?

The passer-by may recover only one-fourth because liability is always divided equally.

The contractor is liable only if all four are sued in the same proceeding.

together or in furtherance of a common design, resulting in damage to another person. Their
liability is joint and several, which means that each tortfeasor is individually liable for the
entire damage and also collectively liable with the others. Independent tortfeasors, on the
other hand, act separately and without coordination. Even if their separate acts cause the
same injury, their liability arises from separate causes of action. In The Koursk, it was
observed that joint liability requires concerted action towards a common end, and mere
similarity of conduct is not enough.

remedies. In Thompson v. London County Council, damage occurred due to separate negligent
acts of different parties, and the Court held that they were not joint tortfeasors because their
acts were independent. Similarly, in The Koursk, two ships were treated as independent

vicarious liability, or common action. Under agency, if one person authorises another to act on
his behalf, both may be liable for torts committed within that authority. Vicarious liability

content.passageText:
XVI. Over the past few weeks, the sharp slide in the rupee’s exchange rate has stroked a long-
pending debate about the true state of the Indian economy. Be that as it may, the urgent
policy decision before the government and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is whether to
prevent the rupee from further sliding against the US dollar or to let it fall and find its true
level.
For the uninitiated, the rupee’s exchange rate against the US dollar basically changes
depending on the relative demand for the two currencies in the foreign exchange (forex)
markets. If Indians demand more dollars (either to buy foreign goods or to invest in other
countries) than the rupees demanded by foreigners (either to buy Indian goods or to invest in
India) then the relative value (exchange rate) moves in favour of the dollar; that is, rupee’s
exchange rate worsens, as indeed it has done in the recent past. If foreigners demand more
rupees than Indians demand dollars, then the rupee’s exchange rate improves. It goes without
saying then that the worsening of the rupee’s exchange rate is reflective of a weakness of the
Indian economy relative to the rest of the world. Seen from this lens, it makes sense to focus
on bolstering the domestic economy instead of wasting time trying to artificially improve the
rupee’s exchange rate.
Indians can’t hold dollars with them for regular use within the country. As such, even if they
get the dollars on their way back from foreign visits, all dollars flow back to the RBI. This
stash of dollars with the RBI can be employed by the central bank to artificially boost the
rupee’s exchange rate when needed.
Imagine a scenario where US investors decide to pull out billions of dollars from their Indian
investments with a view to either investing the money back in US firms or in firms of some
other countries, say, South Korea. Suppose they sell their stake in Indian companies, take the
rupees they got as a result to the forex market to get dollars; after all they need dollars to
transact outside India. This creates a sudden increase in the supply of rupees (without any
new demand for those rupees) and an increase in the demand for dollars (without any new
supply for dollars). The only way to resolve this situation is if the rupee weakens against the
dollar — in other words, if every additional dollar can be bought by exchanging more rupees
than before.

But the RBI can save the rupee’s exchange rate from falling by selling the dollars it has in the
forex market. If it does so then the increased demand of dollars will be countered by an
increased supply of dollars and the increased supply of rupees will be countered by an
increased demand for rupees (by the RBI in return for the dollars it is selling). This is referred
to as the RBI defending the rupee in the forex market. [Word Count: 495]

content.passageText:
XVII. If you're a New Zealander who has spent time overseas, you’ve probably had someone
comment on the way you speak: that swallowed e and flat i, the whole fush and chups thing ...
the rest of the world thinks we pronounce our vowels a bit funny. Even as a researcher of the
Kiwi accent, it took me a while to wrap my head around the fact that “here” and “hair” aren’t
supposed to rhyme. So where did this local form of spoken English originate, and how did we
come to pronounce our vowels in such a unique way?
It’s clearly a question many people have asked, given the interest in my public talk on the
subject in Auckland this week, part of a project using oral history recordings of Aucklanders
born around the turn of the 20th century. These recordings, now housed in the Auckland
Libraries sound archives, let us listen back in time. When we compare them with modern
recordings, we can trace how our accent has developed across generations. This means going
back to when large numbers of English-speaking settlers arrived in Aotearoa New Zealand
from the mid-19th century. Because they came from different parts of Britain — largely the
South of England, Scotland and Ireland — they didn’t all speak the same kind of English and
brought their regional accents with them.
Despite the protests of educational authorities and elocution teachers of the time, what
followed wasn’t the adoption of a single “correct” way of speaking the “Queen’s English”.
Instead, these various accents came into contact, mixed together and gradually levelled out to
something new — not quite British, not quite anything else. New Zealand linguists have known
this part of the story for a while. What we don’t know are some of the specifics. Why, for
example, does our accent have relatively little regional variation (other than Southlanders and

their rolled Rs), despite many early centres such as Christchurch and Dunedin having distinct
cultural identities?
We also don’t know if the accent developed fastest in certain places. Often, accents change
quickly in cities and then spread. But so far, most of our historical research comes from
recordings of speakers born in small towns. This is where a piece of information that was
almost lost provided some surprising inspiration.www.lawpreptutorial.com
One of the things that stood out was a suggestion the accent was developing most strongly in
the North Island, particularly in Auckland. For one, the city has always been comparatively
cosmopolitan, with people arriving from all over Britain rather than one dominant region.
Secondly, its population grew steadily over time, unlike many other districts which saw booms
and stagnation. Both these factors make a good environment for an accent to develop. [Word
Count: 451]

the-cradle-of-the-kiwi-accent-an-old-theory-gets-a-new-hearing-283047

unemployed" and invites those "tired of pretending everything is fine" to join.

entirely, while only 11% belonged to any political party. Across South Asia, youth-led protests

content.questionText:
A newly elected government, claiming to advance the constitutional ideal of equality, introduces
the Uniform Civic Benefits Act, 2026. Under the Act, every citizen, irrespective of age, disability,
economic background, educational attainment, or social disadvantage, is entitled to receive
identical public benefits and is subjected to identical legal obligations. Defending the legislation,
the government argues that any differentiation among citizens is inherently inconsistent with
equality because Article 14 requires the State to treat all persons exactly alike.
Assuming the government's understanding of equality is accepted, which of the following
propositions would most likely be rejected by contemporary Indian constitutional jurisprudence?
options:
Equality permits differential treatment where distinctions are founded on relevant differences
and bear a legitimate connection with the objective sought to be achieved.

Identical treatment of all persons is the highest manifestation of constitutional equality,
irrespective of differences in circumstances.

Treating unequals alike may, in certain situations, produce substantive inequality rather than
equality.

Constitutional equality is concerned not merely with uniformity of treatment but also with
preventing arbitrary State action.
content.explanation: Option B is correct because it reflects the government's assumption that Article 14 requires the State to treat every person exactly alike irrespective of differences in circumstances. However, the passage recognises that the State may make laws operating differently on different classes of people, provided the principle of equality and equal protection of law is maintained.

The State Legislature enacts the Urban Green Mobility Act, 2026, with the stated objective of
reducing vehicular pollution in densely populated metropolitan areas. Under the Act, only electric
vehicles registered within cities having a population exceeding 50 lakh are exempted from road tax,
while electric vehicles registered in smaller cities and rural areas remain liable to pay the tax.
A group of electric vehicle owners from smaller cities challenge the legislation under Article 14,
arguing that all electric vehicles contribute equally to environmental protection and therefore
should receive identical treatment.
Based on the doctrine of reasonable classification discussed in the passage, which of the following
most strongly supports the constitutional validity of the legislation?
options:
The legislation creates a classification between electric vehicle owners and non-electric vehicle
owners.

Environmental protection is a desirable public objective and therefore any classification made
in pursuit of that objective is automatically constitutional.

The classification is based on city population and has a rational nexus with the objective of
reducing pollution in densely populated areas.

Since taxation falls within the legislative domain of the State, Article 14 scrutiny cannot be
applied to tax legislation.
content.explanation: Option C is correct because the classification is based upon a clear distinguishing factor, namely the population size of cities. This creates an intelligible differentia between electric vehicle owners in highly populated urban centres and those in less populated regions.

content.questionText:
The State of Aryavarta enacts the Judicial Efficiency and Expedited Trials Act, 2026, with the
stated objective of reducing the pendency of criminal cases involving economic offences exceeding
210 crore. The Act provides that only persons accused of such offences shall be tried before Special
Fast-Track Courts, while all other criminal cases shall continue to be heard before ordinary
criminal courts.
Several accused persons challenge the legislation under Article 14, arguing that all accused
persons form a single class and cannot be subjected to different procedural treatment merely
because of the nature or value of the alleged offence.
Based on the doctrine of reasonable classification discussed in the passage, which of the following
would most strongly support the constitutional validity of the Act?
options:
The classification is based on the nature and value of the alleged offence and is rationally
connected to expediting complex economic crime trials.

The Act is constitutionally valid because the legislature possesses complete discretion in
matters concerning judicial administration and criminal procedure.

The Act is constitutional because economic offences are generally viewed more seriously by
society than other offences.

The Act is constitutional because Article 14 permits every classification made by the legislature
so long as the classification is expressly stated in the statute.
content.explanation: Option A is correct because the Act classifies accused persons on the basis of a clear and identifiable criterion, namely economic offences exceeding 210 crore. This constitutes an intelligible differentia.

Match the situations in Column I with the constitutional concepts in Column II.
Column I
P. A law grants a housing subsidy exclusively to economically weaker families with annual
incomes below 22 lakh, with the objective of improving access to affordable housing.

bicycles, without any explanation connecting handedness to public safety.

special procedural framework designed to expedite complex trials.
S. A law imposes a higher environmental compliance burden on industries located within
ecologically fragile zones in order to preserve biodiversity.
Column II
1. Classification likely to fail because the grouping appears arbitrary or artificial.
2. Classification supported by an intelligible differentia and rational nexus.
3. Classification based on relevant economic distinctions.
4. Classification based upon geographical circumstances connected to the legislative objective.
Which of the following correctly matches Column I with Column II?

For several decades, challenges under Article 14 were predominantly examined through the lens of
reasonable classification, requiring courts to determine whether a law was founded upon an
intelligible differentia and whether such differentia bore a rational nexus to the object sought to be
achieved. Over time, constitutional courts recognised that certain State actions could satisfy the
formal requirements of classification and yet remain fundamentally incompatible with the
constitutional guarantee of equality.
Which of the following doctrines emerged most significantly to address this limitation in Article 14
jurisprudence?
options:
Doctrine of Eclipse, which permits revival of pre-constitutional laws upon the removal of
constitutional inconsistencies.

Doctrine of Territorial Nexus, which enables legislatures to enact laws having extra-territorial
operation when a sufficient connection exists.

Doctrine against Arbitrariness, which recognises that arbitrary State action may violate
equality even in the absence of an impermissible classification.

Doctrine of Pith and Substance, which determines the true nature and character of legislation
in cases involving legislative competence.
content.explanation: Option C is correct because Article 14 jurisprudence gradually evolved beyond the traditional doctrine of reasonable classification. Courts recognised that a law or State action may satisfy the formal requirements of classification and still be unconstitutional if it is arbitrary.

which the data protection framework revolved. This included the Information Technology
(Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules,
2011 (Privacy Rules).
In 2017, a constitutional bench of nine judges of the Supreme Court of India in Justice K. S.
Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India upheld that privacy is a fundamental right, which is
entrenched in Article 21 [Right to Life & Liberty] of the Constitution of India. This led to the
process of formulation of a comprehensive data protection framework for India. After releasing
different draft versions of a data protection legislation and considering the recommendations from
different stakeholders, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY),
Government of India, released the draft of the Digital Personal Data Protection Bill in 2022 (DPDP
Bill).
The version of the DPDP Bill which was eventually passed by both houses of the Indian Parliament
marked a few significant changes to the original draft of the DPDP Bill. On August 11, 2023, the
Government of India published that version as the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
(DPDP Act), which would form the personal data protection and regulatory regime in India. The
DPDP Act introduces several compliances with respect to the collection, processing, storage and
transfer of digital personal data. However, further actions on behalf of the Government are
required to make the DPDP Act effective, including notifying the sections of the DPDP Act itself,
repealing the Privacy Rules and notifying the rules and regulations required for effective
implementation and enforcement of the DPDP Act. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The DPDP Act is applicable only to personal data in digital form and does not regulate non-
personal and non-digital data. Considering this, collection and handling of non-personal data is
currently unregulated in India.

The current privacy regime is contained within the IT Act and the Privacy Rules. While the
Government of India has released a draft of the rules under the DPDP Act, the provisions of the
Act itself have not yet come into force.

Til.	He was from Ghazipur — sharp, funny, full of ambition — and then, gradually, he wasn't, his
transformation arriving not in a single moment but in the slow, creeping way that addiction always
announces itself, until one day it was complete, and he had joined the thousands around Banaras
Hindu University consumed by a trade that operated with political protection and near-tot: al
impunity in a district that Amitav Ghosh chose, for good reason, as the opening of his Opium War
trilogy, a place where heroin flowed outward from Myanmar through the Ghazipur syndicate and
money and influence flowed back, where the Narcotics Control Bureau launched sustained
campaigns and the trade grew anyway, moving from streets into colleges, from colleges in to
families, until it became too large to confront and was quietly filed away as someone else's problem,
happening to someone else's children, in someone else's district. This is the inheritance th: at
Jammu and Kashmir carries in an even more structurally entrenched form, bordering the Golden
Crescent of Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Iran, where heroin and brown sugar flow through supp ly
networks that now extend drone deliveries into Punjab and Rajasthan, where the trafficking of
narcotics and the trafficking of weapons are rarely separate enterprises, together funding a low-
cost, long-duration campaign of destabilisation that no conventional security operation can easily
reverse, and where the connection between drug money and the financing of separatism has been
long suspected and even longer avoided by a political class with neither the appetite nor the
courage to engage it honestly. Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha's campaign to eradicate dru gs
from the lives of young people in the valley deserves to be taken seriously precisely because his
credentials are not administrative but personal — he is from Ghazipur, he was a student leader at
BHU during the years when the trade was most devastating, and he has seen at close quarte rs
what a generation looks like when it is lost — and the enthusiastic community response his
campaign has drawn, from parents, young people, and civic groups, suggests that people across the
valley are ready to believe that change is possible, which is itself a precondition for change. The
deeper question is whether this energy can be institutionalised and whether the model travels,
because in Ghazipur, in Varanasi, in Punjab, in every city where this quiet catastrophe unfolds
behind closed doors and in whispered family grief, the students lost to addiction deserve nothing
less than the same political will, sustained funding, and unglamorous, patient commitment that no
rally can substitute for and no rhetoric can replace.
content.questionText: The passage best demonstrates which one of the following motifs?
options: Addiction's political entrenchment and hope through sustained committed institutional reform.
Individual redemption through Sinha's courageous personal campaign against drug addiction.
Catastrophic human cost of politically protected and institutionally neglected addiction.

Security operations' consistent failure to reverse cross-border narcotics destabilisation
effectively.
content.explanation: Addiction's political entrenchment and hope through sustained committed institutional reform. — Correct.

evidence.explanation: Addiction's political entrenchment and hope through sustained committed institutional reform. — Correct.

IV.	Dowry-related fatalities reliably trigger choreographed cycles of legislative indignation,
prosecutorial posturing, and performative collective mourning — yet the socioeconomic
substructure that inexorably generates such violence emerges from each episode of public outrage
structurally uncontested, institutionally reinforced, and culturally resanctified. This recursive
contradiction constitutes perhaps the most consequential and deliberately unacknowledged market
failure embedded within India's social economy: a polity that statutorily criminalises dowry while
systematically legitimising its operational logic through euphemistic reclassification — financial
extractions repackaged as familial gifting, status capitalisation, or economically rational
compensation accruing to the male-headed provisioning household. Matrimony in India functions
less as a voluntary interpersonal arrangement than as a sophisticated multi-dimensional
institution — concurrently executing caste boundary enforcement, intergenerational capital
transfer, gendered labour allocation, and hierarchical social mobility negotiation. Within this
institutional architecture, transactional expectations are not peripheral aberrations but
structurally determined outputs of the system's own internal logic. Violence, therefore, resists
analytical disaggregation from the institution itself; it represents the most visible downstream
manifestation of legitimised economic asymmetry, operationalised within household units where
women disproportionately absorb unremunerated care labour, sacrifice professional capital, and
bear asymmetric responsibility for relational preservation — a systematically feminised
productivity cost that neither markets price nor policymakers adequately account for. The
institution's more insidious coercive mechanisms operate beneath the threshold of juridical
visibility entirely: the manufactured social panic surrounding unmarried women of advancing age,
the structural delegitimisation of alternative domesticity arrangements, and the categorical
expectation that intimacy, economic security, and social belonging must be accessed exclusively
through sanctioned matrimonial channels. What presents phenomenologically as autonomous
individual choice routinely operates within profoundly constrained decision environments where
viable structural alternatives have been methodically denied institutional recognition, resource
allocation, and cultural legitimacy. Legislative intervention, however procedurally indispensable,
addresses symptomatic manifestations while leaving foundational determinants operationally
undisturbed. Substantive reform demands something considerably more architecturally disruptive
— the deliberate redistribution of care infrastructure, the institutional scaffolding of collective
living arrangements, and the political willingness to systematically decouple human dignity,
belonging, and security from their near-total dependence upon the privatised matrimonial
household as civilisation's singular legitimate organising unit.

Legislative criminalisation of dowry has substantially disrupted matrimony's transactional
institutional logic nationally.

Matrimony embeds structural transactional logic making dowry violence a downstream
institutional manifestation.

V.	20:26 hours, April 6th, 2026, is a moment that will remain etched in national history, as India's
500 Megawatt Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at (1), successfully attained first criticality,
which is the start of a controlled fission chain reaction. This marked India's long-awaited foray into
the second stage of its three-stage Nuclear power programme. Envisioned in 1954 by eminent
physicist Homi Jehangir Bhabha, India's three-stage Nuclear power programme is aimed at
achieving energy security using the country's limited Uranium and vast Thorium reserves.
A reactor going critical is the culmination of a long process; the PFBR has been in the works for
more than two decades. Usually, there is a gap of several months between fuel being loaded into a
nuclear reactor and the reactor going critical. During the months after fuel loading, a series of
engineering and physics tests are carried out to validate a host of parameters. While criticality is a
major step in the commencement of operations at a nuclear power plant, it does not mean that it
has begun generating power at its full potential. Power generation is ramped up gradually in a
phased manner.
The technology development and design of PFBR was indigenously done by the Indira Gandhi
Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR), an R&D Centre of the Indian Government's Department of
Atomic Energy. The PFBR was built and commissioned by (2), a Government firm.

500 Megawatt Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at (1), successfully attained first criticality,
which is the start of a controlled fission chain reaction. This marked India's long-awaited foray into
the second stage of its three-stage Nuclear power programme. Envisioned in 1954 by eminent
physicist Homi Jehangir Bhabha, India's three-stage Nuclear power programme is aimed at
achieving energy security using the country's limited Uranium and vast Thorium reserves.
A reactor going critical is the culmination of a long process; the PFBR has been in the works for
more than two decades. Usually, there is a gap of several months between fuel being loaded into a
nuclear reactor and the reactor going critical. During the months after fuel loading, a series of
engineering and physics tests are carried out to validate a host of parameters. While criticality is a
major step in the commencement of operations at a nuclear power plant, it does not mean that it
has begun generating power at its full potential. Power generation is ramped up gradually in a
phased manner.
The technology development and design of PFBR was indigenously done by the Indira Gandhi
Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR), an R&D Centre of the Indian Government's Department of
Atomic Energy. The PFBR was built and commissioned by (2), a Government firm.

VI.	In what was a foregone conclusion, the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 failed to secure
the two-thirds majority required for a constitutional amendment. While 298 members voted in its
favour and 230 against, the Bill needed 352 votes — two-thirds of the 528 present and voting — to
pass. The government subsequently shelved the companion Delimitation Bill and the Union
Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, saying they could not be viewed in isolation. During his reply
to the debate, Home Minister Amit Shah gave a verbal guarantee that southern States would see
their presence in an 816-member Lok Sabha increase in the same proportion as their current
share, even offering to adjourn the House for an hour to redraft the Bill with a 50% uniform
increase as an official amendment. The Opposition dismissed this. The obvious question: if
proportional increase was always the intent, why was it not in the Bill? The language as tabled
clearly mandated delimitation on the basis of the latest Census — currently 2011 — which would
have reduced the share of southern, eastern, and northeastern States due to their lower population
growth relative to the Hindi heartland States. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Why the haste to push through a controversial constitutional amendment when the 2026-27
Census is still under way? Also, there was no reason to link women’s reservation, on which there is
all-party consensus, to delimitation in this manner. The bizarre smoke-and-mirrors approach, no
doubt intended to confuse and divide the Opposition, made a mockery of the parliamentary process.
Source: https://www.thehindu.com/opinion/editorial/deservedly-dead-the-hindu-editorial-on-the-
defeat-of-the-constitution-131st-amendment-bill-2026/article70875239.ece

content.passageText:
VI. The mathematical equations governing black holes existed as immutable truths long before such
cosmic phenomena themselves came into being — a proposition that cleaves directly through one of
philosophy's most contentious fault lines: the nature of mathematics itself. Staunch Platonists
contend that mathematical structures, from foundational axioms to elegant geometric constructs
like the tetrahedron, possess an existence wholly independent of human cognition, constituting not
merely a descriptive language of humanity's own fabrication, but rather the very ontological
substrate upon which reality is constructed. Their adversaries, however, vehemently assert that
mathematics is an exclusively anthropogenic enterprise — a sophisticated intellectual scaffolding
imposed upon a universe that would remain utterly indifferent to its absence. Sergiu Klainerman,
distinguished professor of mathematics at Princeton University, positions himself unequivocally
within the former tradition, maintaining that mathematical truth antedates human consciousness,
and that the mathematician's vocation is fundamentally one of excavation rather than invention.
His monumental contributions — including landmark proofs establishing the stability of vacuous
space and the structural resilience of black holes under perturbation — represent, in his firm
conviction, discoveries of pre-existing eternal verities rather than intellectual constructions. To
conflate the invented instruments of mathematical inquiry with the discovered truths they
illuminate constitutes, for Klainerman, a categorical error of profound epistemic consequence. Born
and raised in Communist Romania, Klainerman gravitated toward mathematics during his
undergraduate studies at the University of Bucharest in 1969, drawn not merely by prodigious
aptitude but by something considerably more existential: in a society saturated with ideological
coercion, mathematics alone offered an inviolable sanctuary of pure, uncompromising truth,
entirely beyond the authoritarian reach of Nicolae Ceausescu's regime. This philosophical
conviction was not cultivated in academic discourse but forged through lived experience — a young
man who had witnessed a totalitarian state attempt to subjugate truth itself, discovering in one
discipline an absolute that no political apparatus could manipulate. Dissatisfied with his
university's prevailing pedagogical orthodoxy — which demanded rote assimilation of technical
knowledge while perpetually deferring genuine conceptual understanding — Klainerman sought
intellectual nourishment through an informal study group led by the promising mathematician
Otto Liess, where he encountered partial differential equations: the mathematical language
describing the continuous transformation of physical phenomena across space and time, from
thermal conduction to the evolution of gravitational fields. These sessions, though imperfect in

their own right, proved irrevocably decisive, inaugurating his lifelong immersion in the analytical
framework that would ultimately underpin his celebrated investigations into shock waves, spatial
stability, and black hole dynamics. Yet Klainerman's intellectual ascent unfolded against the
suffocating constraints of life under totalitarianism — constraints compounded considerably by his
Jewish identity, which had already systematically circumscribed his father's distinguished medical
career and now threatened to extinguish his own scholarly ambitions entirely.
content.questionText: What is the central idea being conveyed by the author in the passage?
options: Mathematics is merely a human invention shaped by cultural forces.
Mathematical truths exist independently and are discovered rather than invented.
Klainerman's political oppression drove him to pursue advanced academic mathematics.
Partial differential equations form the foundation of all mathematical understanding.
content.explanation: Mathematical truths exist independently and are discovered rather than invented. — Correct.

evidence.explanation: Mathematical truths exist independently and are discovered rather than invented. — Correct.

VIII. Anyone who has navigated parenthood in the contemporary era will readily attest that childrearing
has become inextricably entwined with perpetual digital consultation, and it is precisely this
phenomenon that Simon Rogers — data editor at Google and former journalist — endeavours to
chronicle in What We Ask Google, an ambitious if ultimately constrained attempt to distil two
decades of anonymised search queries into what the subtitle optimistically characterises as "a
surprisingly hopeful picture of humankind." Drawing upon Google Trends data extending as far
back as 2004, Rogers assembles a thematically organised compendium of collective human
curiosity, ranging from the delightfully mundane — the perennial supremacy of burrito-folding
queries over trouser-folding, disrupted only fleetingly by a 2019 Marie Kondo Netflix phenomenon
— to the intermittently poignant, treating search behaviour as a sociological mirror capable of
reflecting something genuine and substantive about human nature. Certain trends resist all
rational elucidation: why Austrians, Nigerians, and Canadians disproportionately query nocturnal
back pain, or why Kansans most frequently solicit Google's orthographic assistance with "chaos"
while their Missourian neighbours are most confounded by "unconscious," remains entirely opaque.
Where contextual scaffolding is available, Rogers deploys it effectively — noting, for instance, that
early 2023 witnessed search interest in parental caregiving overtaking child-related queries, a
telling demographic testament to the mounting pressures upon the so-called "sandwich
generation." The book's most arresting visual — a cartographic rendering of the 2024 solar eclipse's
trajectory, overlaid with regional spikes in searches pairing "eyes" and "hurt" — speaks eloquently
to the intellectual limitations of certain searchers. However, the work is fundamentally
compromised by its conspicuous omissions and its author's institutional allegiances: Rogers, who
migrated to Google from Twitter in 2015, offers a conspicuously rose-tinted appraisal of the
corporation's broader societal footprint, providing negligible acknowledgment of artificial
intelligence's seismic disruption of search behaviour, the cascading economic devastation inflicted
upon digital publishers by Al-generated summaries, or the considerable role that Silicon Valley's
technological apparatus has played in amplifying the very parental anxieties he catalogues with
such apparent sympathy. The complete absence of any engagement with political search behaviour,
Donald Trump, or humankind's demonstrably darker digital impulses further exposes the selective
nature of Rogers' curation. His interpretive generosity occasionally collapses into naivety — most
egregiously when he frames the high frequency of plasma donation queries as altruistic impulse
rather than as damning evidence of the grotesque socioeconomic inequities endemic to the
American healthcare system. What remains is a diverting, if editorially circumscribed, aperture
onto collective human preoccupation — suitable bathroom reading, though one should approach its
optimistic conclusions with considerable scepticism.
content.questionText: The expression "rose-tinted appraisal" as used in the passage refers to which of the following?
options: Rogers' unrealistically optimistic portrayal of Google's broader societal cultural influence.
Rogers' deliberate omission of politically contentious and controversial analytical topics.
Rogers' superficial engagement with complex socioeconomic inequities within American society.
Rogers' selective deployment of search data to construct a misleadingly hopeful narrative.
content.explanation: Rogers' unrealistically optimistic portrayal of Google's broader societal cultural influence. — Correct.

evidence.explanation: Rogers' unrealistically optimistic portrayal of Google's broader societal cultural influence. — Correct.

XI.	Meaningful progress in reducing urban traffic congestion cannot be achieved within the current
fragmented model of municipal transport planning, in which infrastructure investment decisions
are made independently by dozens of separate local councils within each metropolitan region. The
reason is that this model creates strong incentives for each council to minimise infrastructure
expenditure within its own boundaries while directing commuter flows toward neighbouring
jurisdictions, thereby shifting the effective cost of managing peak-hour congestion onto adjacent
councils or the regional government. That is precisely the pattern demonstrated by the various
transport decentralisation experiments of the 2000s: relieve congestion on one arterial corridor and
an equally severe bottleneck emerges elsewhere. For example, when one inner-city council invested
in expanded bus rapid transit capacity, peak-hour vehicle flows simply shifted to parallel arterial
roads managed by the neighbouring council.

options:
Under the conditions in which the current fragmented municipal transport planning model
operates, meaningful reduction in regional traffic congestion could be achieved, if at all, only
through a coordinated regional transport authority with unified investment decision-making
powers.

Individual local councils are primarily motivated by the desire to maximise their own
infrastructure grant allocations rather than to achieve measurable improvements in regional
traffic flow.

Regional transport infrastructure expenditure tends to expand automatically to absorb
additional funding made available through special purpose congestion relief grants from state
governments.

Since underutilised bus rapid transit corridors contribute to per-passenger operating cost
increases, it would be imprudent for councils to maintain reserve capacity for managing major
public events.
content.explanation: Under the conditions in which the current fragmented municipal transport planning model operates, meaningful reduction in regional traffic congestion could be achieved, if at all, only through a coordinated regional transport authority with unified investment decision-making powers. — Correct.

content.passageText:
XII. Fraud, as elucidated in Section 17 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, implies and involves any of the
acts mentioned below perpetrated by a contracting party or with his involvement or by his agent
with the objective of deceiving or misleading another party or his agent to enter into the
agreement. The acts which constitute fraud under this provision are as follows:- The suggestion, as
a fact, of something which is not true by someone who does not believe in its truth. The active
concealment of a fact by one having knowledge or belief of the fact. A promise without any intent of
carrying it out. Any other act which may mislead the other party. An act or omission which the law
specifically declares to be fraudulent. Mere silence in relation to facts which may influence the
willingness of a person to enter into a contract is not fraud. However, if the circumstances of the
case are such that, having regard to them, it is the duty of the person keeping silent to speak, or
unless his silence, is in itself, equivalent to speech, in such circumstances the silence itself may be
deemed fraudulent. Section 17 explains fraud and mentions the acts that amount to fraud, which
are a false suggestion, active concealment, promise lacking any intention of carrying it out, any
other deceptive act, or any act declared fraudulent. In the English case, Derry vs. Peek (1889), it
was said that, “fraud” is proved when it is shown that a false representation has been made:
Knowingly, or Without belief in its truth, or Recklessly careless whether it be true or false. In
simple terms, “fraud” refers to deliberate deception perpetrated with the intent to induce another
party to act to their detriment. As far as contracts are concerned, fraud can manifest in various
forms such as false representations, concealment of facts, deceptive claims etc.
Source: Extracted with edits from https://blog.ipleaders.in/fraud-in-contracts-section-17-of-the-
indian-contract-act/
content.questionText:
A collector offers to sell an antique coin to Y for %5 lakh. The collector is aware that a leading
auction house recently authenticated the coin as a rare historical artifact worth nearly 750 lakh.
During negotiations, Y specifically asks whether there is any information known to the collector
that could materially affect the coin's value. The collector remains silent and proceeds with the
sale. Later, Y discovers the auction-house report and seeks to avoid the contract on the ground of
fraud.
Which of the following most accurately reflects the legal position?
options:
The collector's silence cannot amount to fraud because mere silence regarding facts affecting
willingness to contract is never fraudulent.

The collector's silence may amount to fraud because, once directly questioned on a material
fact, the circumstances created a duty to speak.

The collector's silence amounts to fraud only if the coin was ultimately sold for less than its
market value.

The collector's silence constitutes active concealment because withholding material information
may itself amount to deception.
content.explanation: Option B is correct because although mere silence ordinarily does not amount to fraud, the passage recognises an important exception. Where the circumstances create a duty to disclose material information, silence may itself become fraudulent.

evidence.explanation: Option B is correct because although mere silence ordinarily does not amount to fraud, the passage recognises an important exception. Where the circumstances create a duty to disclose material information, silence may itself become fraudulent.
