content.questionText:
A real-estate developer enters into agreements with several purchasers, promising that a
residential project will be completed within two years. Internal company emails, existing at the
time of contracting, reveal that the developer had already decided to abandon the project because
regulatory approval was impossible to obtain. Nevertheless, the agreements were executed and
advance payments accepted.
Which of the following best explains why the developer's conduct may amount to fraud?
options: Every breach of a contractual promise automatically constitutes fraud.
Fraud arises because the project was ultimately not completed.
A promise made without any intention of performing it may amount to fraud.
Fraud arises whenever a contracting party suffers financial loss.
content.explanation: Option C is correct because the passage expressly recognises as fraud a promise made without any intention of performing it. In the present case, the developer had already decided to abandon the project before entering into the agreements and accepting advance payments.

content.questionText:
A company director circulates an investment memorandum stating that a newly discovered
technology has already received regulatory approval. At the time of making the statement, the
director has not verified the information and has no basis for believing it to be true. Nevertheless,
he proceeds to make the representation because he assumes the approval "probably exists."
Applying the principle laid down in Derry v. Peek (1889), which of the following factors most
strongly supports a finding of fraud?
options: The director genuinely believed the statement to be true, although it later proved inaccurate.
The investors suffered substantial financial loss after relying on the statement.
The representation was made recklessly without caring whether it was true or false.
The representation was made during the course of a commercial transaction.
content.explanation: Option C is correct because the facts indicate that the director had no basis for believing the statement to be true and made the representation without verifying its accuracy. He proceeded merely on an assumption that approval "probably existed." This demonstrates reckless disregard for the truth of the statement.

content.passageText:
XIV. The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation is an important principle of constitutional law that prevents
legislatures from indirectly doing what they are not permitted to do directly. It is often described as
a “fraud on the Constitution” because it checks attempts by legislative bodies to exceed their
constitutional authority while appearing to act within legal limits. The doctrine originates from the
Latin maxim “quando aliquid prohibetur ex directo, prohibetur et per obliquum,” which means that
what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. In India, this doctrine was adopted from
Canadian and Australian constitutional practices during British rule and later became an integral
part of constitutional jurisprudence after independence. The doctrine primarily examines the
legislative competence of Parliament and State Legislatures.
It comes into operation when a legislature enacts a law on a subject over which it has no authority,
but disguises the legislation in a manner that makes it appear valid. The courts then look beyond
the form of the law to determine its real substance and purpose. If the true nature of the legislation
reveals that the legislature has trespassed into a field outside its constitutional powers, the law
may be declared void. This doctrine is closely linked to Article 246 of the Constitution of India,
which distributes legislative powers between the Union and the States through the Union List,
State List, and Concurrent List. By applying this doctrine, courts ensure that neither Parliament
nor State Legislatures encroach upon each other’s constitutionally assigned domains.
However, the doctrine has certain limitations. It applies only to questions of legislative competence
and not to the wisdom, necessity, or motives behind a law. It is also generally inapplicable where
there are no constitutional restrictions on legislative power and does not usually extend to
subordinate legislation. The intention of the legislature, whether good or bad, is not the focus; the
only concern is whether the law falls within its constitutional authority. A significant case related
to this doctrine is R.S. Joshi v. Ajit Mills (1977), where the Supreme Court clarified that colourable
legislation arises when a legislature lacks the power to enact a law but attempts to create the
appearance of possessing such authority. Thus, the doctrine serves as an essential safeguard for
maintaining constitutional balance and federal governance in India.
Source: Extracted with edits from https://blog.ipleaders.in/doctrine-of-colourable-legislation/
content.questionText:
The Constitution places "Agriculture" in the State List and "Inter-State Trade and Commerce" in
the Union List. Concerned about food security, Parliament enacts the National Agricultural Supply
Stabilisation Act, 2026. The Act is stated to regulate the movement of agricultural products across
state borders. However, its provisions require farmers to obtain cultivation permits from a Central
Authority, prescribe the crops that may be grown in particular districts, regulate irrigation
practices on private farms, and authorize the Central Authority to inspect agricultural lands.
Parliament argues that these measures are necessary to ensure a stable national supply chain and
therefore fall within its power over inter-State trade.
The State of Z challenges the Act, alleging that Parliament has used its power over inter-State
trade as a device to assume control over agriculture. The Union responds that the Act's objective is
national market regulation and that courts cannot question legislative wisdom.
Which of the following is the most constitutionally sound conclusion?
options:
The Act is valid because whenever a law is connected to a Union List subject, courts cannot
examine its practical effect.

The Act is valid because legislative motive is irrelevant, and therefore any challenge based on
colourable legislation must fail.

The Act may be struck down if the court finds that, in substance, Parliament is regulating
agriculture under the guise of regulating inter-State trade.

The Act must be upheld because food security is a matter of national importance and
automatically overrides the distribution of legislative powers.
content.explanation: This option correctly applies the doctrine. The court would examine the substance over form of the legislation.

Parliament enacts the National Digital Security Act, 2027 to regulate online platforms. The Act
requires all social media companies to store user data on servers located within India, comply with
government cybersecurity standards, and submit periodic security audits. Several technology
companies challenge the law, arguing that the real objective of Parliament is to increase
governmental control over private digital communications rather than cybersecurity. They contend
that the law is therefore a colourable exercise of legislative power.
Assume that Parliament unquestionably possesses constitutional authority to legislate on digital
communications and cybersecurity.
Which of the following is the most appropriate constitutional conclusion?
options: The Act is colourable legislation because its actual objective differs from its stated objective.

The Act is colourable legislation because courts may invalidate any law enacted with an
ulterior motive.

The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation is unlikely to apply because Parliament possesses
legislative competence.

The Act is automatically unconstitutional because governmental control over communications
violates the doctrine.
content.explanation: The doctrine applies when a legislature lacks authority and attempts to achieve indirectly what it cannot do directly. Here, Parliament unquestionably has competence over the subject matter.

the legislative competence of Parliament under the Union List. Parliament enacts the National
Carbon Emissions Regulation Act, 2028, requiring all manufacturing companies to obtain emission
permits and comply with nationwide environmental standards.
The Act significantly increases production costs for industries, causing several factories to shut
down and leading to unemployment in some regions. A group of industrial associations challenges
the law, arguing that although it is framed as environmental legislation, its real effect is to control
industrial activity and economic policy. They contend that the law is therefore a colourable exercise
of legislative power.
Which of the following is the most constitutionally sound conclusion?
options: The Act is colourable because its economic impact extends beyond environmental protection.

The Act is colourable because courts should focus primarily on the consequences of a law rather
than the source of legislative power.
The Act is colourable whenever its practical effects are broader than its stated objective.

The Act is not colourable, provided its true nature remains environmental regulation, a subject
within Parliament's competence.
content.explanation: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The Act is not colourable, provided its true nature remains environmental regulation, a subject within Parliament's competence. Accordingly, option D is the keyed legal result.

content.passageText:
XIV. The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation is an important principle of constitutional law that prevents
legislatures from indirectly doing what they are not permitted to do directly. It is often described as
a “fraud on the Constitution” because it checks attempts by legislative bodies to exceed their
constitutional authority while appearing to act within legal limits. The doctrine originates from the
Latin maxim “quando aliquid prohibetur ex directo, prohibetur et per obliquum,” which means that
what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. In India, this doctrine was adopted from
Canadian and Australian constitutional practices during British rule and later became an integral
part of constitutional jurisprudence after independence. The doctrine primarily examines the
legislative competence of Parliament and State Legislatures.
It comes into operation when a legislature enacts a law on a subject over which it has no authority,
but disguises the legislation in a manner that makes it appear valid. The courts then look beyond
the form of the law to determine its real substance and purpose. If the true nature of the legislation
reveals that the legislature has trespassed into a field outside its constitutional powers, the law
may be declared void. This doctrine is closely linked to Article 246 of the Constitution of India,
which distributes legislative powers between the Union and the States through the Union List,
State List, and Concurrent List. By applying this doctrine, courts ensure that neither Parliament
nor State Legislatures encroach upon each other’s constitutionally assigned domains.
However, the doctrine has certain limitations. It applies only to questions of legislative competence
and not to the wisdom, necessity, or motives behind a law. It is also generally inapplicable where
there are no constitutional restrictions on legislative power and does not usually extend to
subordinate legislation. The intention of the legislature, whether good or bad, is not the focus; the
only concern is whether the law falls within its constitutional authority. A significant case related
to this doctrine is R.S. Joshi v. Ajit Mills (1977), where the Supreme Court clarified that colourable
legislation arises when a legislature lacks the power to enact a law but attempts to create the
appearance of possessing such authority. Thus, the doctrine serves as an essential safeguard for
maintaining constitutional balance and federal governance in India.
Source: Extracted with edits from https://blog.ipleaders.in/doctrine-of-colourable-legislation/

content.questionText:
Suppose the State of Vindhya passes the Digital News Regulation and Public Welfare Act,
2028. The Act requires all online news platforms operating within the State to pay a mandatory
Public Welfare Contribution amounting to 15% of their annual advertising revenue. The money
collected is to be used for healthcare and education projects. The State Legislature claims that the
law concerns public welfare and regulation of local businesses. However, the practical effect of the
law is to impose a financial burden specifically on digital media companies.
Several digital news platforms challenge the law, arguing that the State is actually attempting to
regulate digital communications and online broadcasting, matters that fall within Parliament's
legislative domain. The State responds that the law does not regulate digital communications but
merely raises funds for welfare purposes and that courts should not question legislative motives.
Which of the following is the most accurate legal conclusion?
options:
The law is automatically valid because welfare measures are always within the competence of
State Legislatures.

The law can never be challenged because courts cannot review legislation passed by elected
legislatures.

The law may be struck down as colourable legislation, if it is found that the State is indirectly
regulating on Parliament’s subject.

The law is valid because the legislature described the payment as a "contribution" rather than
a "tax."
content.explanation: A The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation does not focus on whether the objective is good or bad. It focuses on whether the legislature had the constitutional authority to enact the law.

evidence.explanation: A The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation does not focus on whether the objective is good or bad. It focuses on whether the legislature had the constitutional authority to enact the law.

Tribes (ST) population and over regulations on live-in relationships and a demand for wider
consultations before considering the legislation, the Assam Assembly Wednesday passed the
Uniform Civil Code (UCC) Bill, two days after it was tabled in the House. The discussion on the
Bill, which was introduced less than two weeks after the second Himanta Biswa Sarma-led NDA
government was sworn in, lasted over five hours. The Bill — which states that its aim is to “govern
and regulate the laws relating to marriage and divorce, succession, live-in relationships” and
connected matters — was passed amidst protests by Opposition MLAs and a demand that it be sent
to a select committee. During the course of the debate, Congress MLA Jakir Hussain Sikdar had
raised the demand for public consultation before passing the Bill.
“The Central Law Commission had in 2018 said that a UCC is neither necessary nor desirable at
this stage, but that if the government wants to introduce such a step, then consultations have to be
held with the public, religious organisations and political parties. They brought the UCC Bill in the
Assembly, the Cabinet took a decision and the Bill was tabled. But before that, the Assam
government did not hold consultations with the people of the state... They are calling the UCC
historic, so before taking such a historic decision, it can’t be just with the discussion of 126 MLAs in
the Assembly... This Bill should not be passed and should be brought to the Assembly only after
wide consultations with the public and organisations,” he said.

investigative agency has arrested the mastermind and nine other people, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H,

person compulsorily replaces one of the answers (not a blank one) with a wrong answer in his/her
answer key.

content.passageText:
XIX. Contracts of indemnity and contracts of guarantee are special types of contracts under the Indian
Contract Act, 1872 that deal with the allocation of risk and liability. A contract of indemnity,
defined under Section 124 of the Act, is a contract by which one party promises to save another
from loss caused to him by the conduct of the promisor himself or by the conduct of any other
person. In such a contract, there are two parties: the indemnifier (who promises to compensate)
and the indemnified (who is protected from loss). The primary purpose of an indemnity contract is
to provide security against potential loss, and liability arises only when there is actual loss suffered
by the indemnified party. A common example is an insurance contract, where the insurer
indemnifies the insured against specified losses.
On the other hand, a contract of guarantee is defined under Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act
as a contract to perform the promise or discharge the liability of a third person in case of his
default. It involves three parties: the surety (who gives the guarantee), the principal debtor (who
owes the obligation), and the creditor (to whom the guarantee is given). The objective of a
guarantee is to provide assurance to the creditor that the debt or obligation will be fulfilled. Unlike
indemnity, the liability of the surety is secondary and arises only when the principal debtor
defaults. A guarantee may be either oral or written, although in practice it is usually documented.
A surety’s liability is co-extensive and not dependent on prior suit against debtor.
The key difference between indemnity and guarantee lies in the nature of liability and the number
of parties involved. In indemnity, liability is primary and independent, whereas in a guarantee,
liability is secondary and conditional upon default by the principal debtor. Furthermore, indemnity
involves only two parties, while guarantee involves three. Another important distinction is that
indemnity focuses on compensation for loss, whereas guarantee focuses on ensuring performance or
payment of another person’s obligation.
These concepts are widely used in commercial transactions, banking, insurance, and financial
agreements to reduce risk and ensure trust between parties. The Supreme Court of India has also
clarified in various judgments that the distinction between indemnity and guarantee must be
determined based on the substance of the contract rather than its form or title. Thus, both these
contracts play a crucial role in facilitating secured commercial dealings in modern legal systems.
Source: https://lawbhoomi.com/contract-of-indemnity-meaning-concept-and-nature/ and
hittps://lawbhoomi.com/contract-of-guarantee-under-indian-contract-act/
content.questionText:
Aman approaches a bank to secure a loan for his minor son, Kabir. Knowing that a minor is legally
incompetent to contract, the bank refuses. Aman tells the banker, ‘Give him the money. If he does
not pay you back, I will’. The bank lends the money. Based on the substance of this transaction,
what is the nature of this contract?
options: It is a contract of guarantee.
It is a contract of indemnity.

It is a contract of guarantee because there are three distinct parties involved: Aman, Kabir (the
minor), and the lending bank.

It is a void contract altogether because it attempts to circumvent the law regarding a minor’s
incapacity to enter into financial agreements.
content.explanation: Why B is correct: For a contract of guarantee to exist under Section 126, there must be a valid, enforceable primary debt owed by a principal debtor. Since a minor's agreement is void from the very beginning under Indian law, Kabir cannot owe a legal debt.

by the conduct of the promisor himself.

A micro-lending NGO disbursed a loan to a woman entrepreneur, Ms. Kavita, based on a verbal
statement by her neighbour, Mr. Gopal, who said at the time of disbursement: She is reliable, you
can trust her. No formal agreement was entered into with Mr. Gopal, no consideration was given to
him, and he made no promise to repay if Kavita defaulted. Kavita later failed to repay. The NGO
sought to hold Mr. Gopal liable. Which of the following correctly analyses the situation?

Mr. Gopal is liable as a surety because his statement at the time of disbursement implied a
guarantee.
Mr. Gopal is liable because oral guarantees are valid under the Indian Contract Act.

principal debtor's liability on default.

Mr. Gopal is liable under a contract of indemnity as his statement caused the NGO to part with
money.

XXII. A well-established legal theory, proposition, or doctrine that is typically stated in Latin is called
a legal maxim. The majority of these Latin maxims originate from European countries that used
Latin as their official language throughout the middle ages. These guidelines enable courts all over
the world to settle cases before them by applying the law as it stands in a fair and reasonable way.
Although such concepts are not legally binding, they do acquire legal status and provide the basis
for good decisions when courts apply them to decide cases or when the legislature adopts them to
pass laws. www.lawpreptutorial.com
To avoid utilizing lengthy definitions, we refer to it as a single word or phrase. For instance, the
maxim "ab initio," which translates to "from the beginning of" or "from the beginning of anything,"
may be used in place of drafting a statement and is equally helpful in practice. The views of early
English philosophers about the application of legal maxims are praiseworthy. According to Thomas
Hobbes' assertion in "Doctor and Student," legal maxims are just as powerful as laws and actions.
Every act or piece of legislation is drafted with a specific goal in mind. Interpreting the provisions
so as to avoid obstructing the lawmakers' intent is a significant duty of the judiciary. By providing
a framework and criteria for interpreting the law, legal maxims play a crucial role in supporting
the court.

interpretation-and-judicial-decisions/

a legal maxim. The majority of these Latin maxims originate from European countries that used

so as to avoid obstructing the lawmakers' intent is a significant duty of the judiciary. By providing
a framework and criteria for interpreting the law, legal maxims play a crucial role in supporting
the court.

content.passageText:
XXIII. The controversy erupted through channels that have become depressingly familiar: perceptive
readers identified conspicuously algorithmic prose within a published literary work, unleashed
their derision across social media platforms, and deployed Al-detection software that returned
damning verdicts — precipitating institutional paralysis among the organisations responsible for
the work's publication. At the epicentre stood Jamir Nazir, a virtually obscure Trinidadian writer
whose short story "The Serpent in the Grove" had secured regional recognition within the
prestigious Commonwealth Short Story Prize, earning both a £2,500 honorarium and publication in
Granta, the esteemed British literary journal — before online scrutineers gleefully dissected its
suspiciously mechanical cadences, its formulaic syntactic constructions, and its grotesquely
overwrought metaphors. Suspicion rapidly metastasised to encompass two additional prizewinners:
Malta's John Edward DeMicoli and India's Sharon Aruparayil, both of whose stories were flagged
by Al-detection platforms as substantially or entirely machine-generated. Aruparayil, uniquely
among the accused, issued a categorical denial, insisting that no artificial intelligence had

participated in any dimension of her creative process, though she conspicuously declined to furnish
the time-stamped manuscript drafts she claimed as exculpatory evidence — whilst separately
disavowing an Al-promoting blog post attributed to her by an Emirati research foundation. What
distinguishes this particular scandal from its predecessors is not the institutional embarrassment
of unwittingly platforming Al-generated literature — a phenomenon that has infiltrated outlets as
venerable as The New York Times and publishing houses of considerable distinction — but rather
the authors' unprecedented and collective refusal to acknowledge any algorithmic involveme nt
whatsoever. The Commonwealth Foundation's director general, Razmi Farook, opted for
circumspection over rigour, accepting the prizewinners' reassurances while explicitly
acknowledging that her organisation's legal constraints precluded challenging an author's stated
honesty purely on the basis of detector outputs. Granta's response proved equally equivocal — and
considerably more farcical — when its publisher elected to consult the AI chatbot Claude for an
adjudication on suspected AI authorship, a methodological absurdity that predictably intensified
rather than ameliorated public ridicule. The deeper systemic vulnerability exposed by this episode
is not merely technological but institutional: given that Al-detection platforms remain
demonstrably fallible — exhibiting documented false-positive biases against non-native English
writers — and given that rescinding literary prizes without incontrovertible evidence carries
formidable moral and legal implications, determined authors may have identified a pote nt
enforcement loophole. Meanwhile, scholars Emily Bender and Alex Hanna advocate something
rather more immediate: sustained, unapologetic public ridicule of derivative, algorithmically
hollowed prose as both cultural resistance and prophylactic standard-maintenance — a strategy
that, however informal, may ultimately prove more efficacious than any institutional review panel
in preserving the irreducibly human essence of authentic literary creation.
content.questionText: Why has the author described the AI literary scandal as "depressingly familiar"?
options: Because AI detection tools consistently produce false positives in literature.
Because social media always overreacts to unverified literary plagiarism accusations.
Because publishers have repeatedly failed to screen Al-generated literary submissions.
Because prior scandals followed identical patterns of detection and denial.
content.explanation: Because prior scandals followed identical patterns of detection and denial. — Correct.

the work's publication. At the epicentre stood Jamir Nazir, a virtually obscure Trinidadian writer
whose short story "The Serpent in the Grove" had secured regional recognition within the
prestigious Commonwealth Short Story Prize, earning both a £2,500 honorarium and publication in
Granta, the esteemed British literary journal — before online scrutineers gleefully dissected its
suspiciously mechanical cadences, its formulaic syntactic constructions, and its grotesquely
overwrought metaphors. Suspicion rapidly metastasised to encompass two additional prizewinners:
Malta's John Edward DeMicoli and India's Sharon Aruparayil, both of whose stories were flagged
by Al-detection platforms as substantially or entirely machine-generated. Aruparayil, uniquely
among the accused, issued a categorical denial, insisting that no artificial intelligence had

participated in any dimension of her creative process, though she conspicuously declined to furnish
the time-stamped manuscript drafts she claimed as exculpatory evidence — whilst separately
disavowing an Al-promoting blog post attributed to her by an Emirati research foundation. What
distinguishes this particular scandal from its predecessors is not the institutional embarrassment
of unwittingly platforming Al-generated literature — a phenomenon that has infiltrated outlets as
venerable as The New York Times and publishing houses of considerable distinction — but rather
the authors' unprecedented and collective refusal to acknowledge any algorithmic involveme nt
whatsoever. The Commonwealth Foundation's director general, Razmi Farook, opted for
circumspection over rigour, accepting the prizewinners' reassurances while explicitly
acknowledging that her organisation's legal constraints precluded challenging an author's stated
honesty purely on the basis of detector outputs. Granta's response proved equally equivocal — and
considerably more farcical — when its publisher elected to consult the AI chatbot Claude for an
adjudication on suspected AI authorship, a methodological absurdity that predictably intensified
rather than ameliorated public ridicule. The deeper systemic vulnerability exposed by this episode
is not merely technological but institutional: given that Al-detection platforms remain
demonstrably fallible — exhibiting documented false-positive biases against non-native English
writers — and given that rescinding literary prizes without incontrovertible evidence carries
formidable moral and legal implications, determined authors may have identified a pote nt
enforcement loophole. Meanwhile, scholars Emily Bender and Alex Hanna advocate something
rather more immediate: sustained, unapologetic public ridicule of derivative, algorithmically
hollowed prose as both cultural resistance and prophylactic standard-maintenance — a strategy
that, however informal, may ultimately prove more efficacious than any institutional review panel
in preserving the irreducibly human essence of authentic literary creation.

Train literary judges to recognise characteristic stylistic AI prose markers.
Recognise that both institutional and technological constraints jointly enable loopholes.
Develop more culturally sensitive detection tools that eliminate false-positive biases.

XXIV. The defining moral failure of the older generation toward contemporary youth is not, as
conventional wisdom might suggest, one of excessive severity or unreasonable expectation — it is,
far more insidiously, one of catastrophic under-demand, a condescending benevolence that
simultaneously overestimates our character and remains perpetually bewildered by our failure to
meet even its negligible standards. Consider the now-notorious photograph of a UCLA graduate
triumphantly brandishing a ChatGPT interface at his commencement ceremony — an image that
has inspired an exhausting proliferation of superficial commentary content to engage with it at its
most anodyne interpretation: that the student employed artificial intelligence to circumvent
academic assessments and thereby fraudulently obtain his degree. Academic dishonesty is neither
novel nor particularly illuminating as a cultural phenomenon; what is genuinely alarming — and
what virtually every commentator above a certain age demonstrably fails to comprehend — is the
totalising, systemic pervasiveness of AI integration across every stratum of contemporary
university life, a penetration so thorough that characterising it merely as sophisticated cheating
represents a categorical confusion masquerading as moral discernment. The metastatic
proliferation of artificial intelligence across elite American campuses constitutes nothing less than
a civilisational pathology, one threatening to transmute an entire cohort of intellectually capable
young people into a generation of cognitively atrophied dependents, whilst simultaneously
desecrating the university as an institution — whether conceived as a humanist sanctuary, an
ethical formation ground, or a utilitarian credentialing apparatus. The author's own trajectory of
disillusionment at the University of Chicago charts this oncological progression with clinical
precision: what initially manifested as a localised and largely contained phenomenon — fraternity
members receiving mediocre scores on Al-assisted assessments, a logic professor dismissing

ChatGPT's transparently fallacious reasoning -— underwent a _ discernible malignant
transformation, evidenced most starkly by a forty-percentage-point differential between take-home
and in-person examination performance observed during a subsequent teaching assistantship. The
primary site of this cancerous metastasis proved, with grim predictability, to be the business
economics specialisation — a recently instituted and broadly derided academic appendage, widely
regarded by serious students as an intellectually undemanding concession to credentialist
pragmatism — wherein the pedagogical architecture itself seems almost deliberately engineered to
accommodate, if not incentivise, cognitive outsourcing: perfunctorily graded problem sets, recycled
sample examinations, arithmetic of conspicuous simplicity, and lecture-slide reiteration
substituting for genuine intellectual engagement. In such an environment, where conscientious
attendance and authentic intellectual labour are rendered entirely superfluous to the attainment of
acceptable marks, the conditions for wholesale artificial intelligence dependency are not merely
permissive but structurally determinative — a truth whose gravity the generation responsible for
designing these institutions appears constitutionally unable to confront.
content.questionText: | Why has the author called the proliferation of AI across elite campuses a "civilisational pathology"?
options: Because AI enables sophisticated cheating that older generations simply cannot detect.
Because AI renders all established pedagogical methods entirely and irreversibly obsolete.
Because AI threatens to corrode every dimension universities are imagined to serve.

Because AI dependency is most destructively concentrated within business economics
programmes.
content.explanation: Because AI threatens to corrode every dimension universities are imagined to serve. — Correct.

evidence.explanation: Because AI threatens to corrode every dimension universities are imagined to serve. — Correct.

I.	People came to him when the patient was on his last legs. Dr. Raman often burst out, ‘Why
couldn’t you have come a day earlier? The reason was obvious—visiting fee twenty-five rupees,

the scene it was always a quick decision one way or another. There was no scope or time for any
kind of wavering or whitewashing. Long years of practice of this kind had bred in the doctor a
certain curt truthfulness; for that very reason his opinion was valued; he was not a mere doctor
expressing an opinion but a judge pronouncing a verdict. The patient’s life hung on his words. This
never unduly worried Dr. Raman. He never believed that agreeable words ever saved lives. He did
not think it was any of his business to provide comforting lies when as a matter of course nature
would tell them the truth in a few hours. However, when he glimpsed the faintest sign of hope, he
rolled up his sleeve and stepped into the arena: it might be hours or days, but he never withdrew
till he wrested the prize from Yama’s hands.

content.passageText:
II.	The Peshawar and Sholapur episodes during the Civil Disobedience Movement of 1930 revealed
the shifting nature of British colonial authority and the growing fearlessness of the Indian masses.
In Peshawar, the atmosphere became electric when the arrest of local leaders led to a massive
upsurge. Here, a significant event occurred that shook the very foundations of the British Raj: the
refusal of the Garhwali soldiers to fire on their unarmed Muslim compatriots. This instance of
cross-communal and cross-class solidarity among the armed forces indicated that the traditional
instruments of colonial repression were no longer entirely reliable.
Simultaneously, in the industrial town of Sholapur, the movement took a more radical turn.
Following the news of Gandhiji’s arrest, textile workers went on a strike that transformed into a
virtual takeover of the town. For several days, British administration effectively vanished, and the
rebels established a parallel government. This was not merely a protest; it was a demonstration of
the "power of the street" where laborers, often viewed as politically inert, became the vanguard of
the nationalist struggle.
The movement’s strength lay in its unprecedented mobilization of women. For the first time,
women from various socio-economic backgrounds—from affluent urban households to rural
peasant families—marched in processions, picketed liquor shops, and faced lathi charges with
stoic endurance. This shattered the domestic-public divide that had characterized earlier political
phases. Furthermore, the commercial classes, hit hard by the Great Depression, threw their
financial weight behind the Congress, seeing in Swaraj a shield against discriminatory colonial
economic policies.
However, unlike the Non-Cooperation era, communal unity remained fragile. While certain
pockets saw joint participation, the formal distancing of large sections of the Muslim political
leadership created a vacuum that would later be filled by separatist ideologies. Despite this, the
movement proved that Indian nationalism had matured into a sophisticated, multi-layered force
capable of paralyzing the colonial state through disciplined non-violence.
Source: Extracted, with edits and revisions, from India After Gandhi and History of Modern India,
by Ramachandra Guha and Bipin Chandra.

It was the primary reason Gandhiji decided to end the Civil Disobedience Movement.
content.explanation: Option A is historically incorrect. Option C is an overstatement not supported by the text.

Ill. The optimism surrounding the "Third Wave" of democratization was largely predicated on the
belief that information technology would act as an irreversible catalyst for liberty. In the early
2000s, it was argued that the decentralized nature of the internet would make it impossible for
autocratic regimes to control the flow of information. However, the subsequent decade witnessed
the rise of "digital authoritarianism," a sophisticated model where state actors utilize data and
technology to entrench their power rather than relinquish it. This shift has fundamentally altered
the global political landscape, creating what some scholars call a "technological iron curtain."

Central to this transformation is the weaponization of social media and the deployment of
advanced surveillance systems. Unlike the overt repression of the twentieth century, modern
illiberal regimes often employ "informational autocracy," where they manipulate public opinion
through state-sponsored disinformation and algorithmic censorship. This allows the state to
maintain a facade of democratic legitimacy while systematically hollowing out the institutions
that protect civil liberties. Furthermore, the export of surveillance technology from dominant
autocratic powers to developing nations has facilitated a "normative shift," making high-tech
monitoring a standardized tool of governance. www.lawpreptutorial.com
By 2020, the retreat from democratic norms had reached a critical juncture. The promise that
prosperity and global connectivity would naturally lead to liberal outcomes was challenged by the
resilience of state-led capitalism. Freedom House reported that the gap between democratic gains
and losses had widened for the fifteenth consecutive year. The "democratic recession" identified
earlier in the century had evolved into a more profound "democratic depression," characterized by
the erosion of judicial independence and the suppression of independent media in even established
democracies.
Source: Extracted, with edits and revisions, from The Age of Surveillance Capitalism by Shoshana
Zuboff and The Road to Unfreedom by Timothy Snyder.

The initial belief in its role as a tool for liberty has been challenged by its use in state control.

It has successfully created an "iron curtain" that prevents any information from crossing
borders.
It is no longer considered a relevant factor in the study of global political landscapes.
content.explanation: The passage contrasts the early belief in technology as a catalyst for liberty with the current reality of digital authoritarianism.

content.passageText:
IV.	American literature represents a distinct and vigorous tradition that has profoundly shaped the
global literary landscape. From the brooding transcendentalism of Ralph Waldo Emerson to the
gritty realism of Mark Twain and the innovative modernism of F. Scott Fitzgerald, it offers a
diverse exploration of the "American Dream" and its inherent contradictions. A foundational figure
is Nathaniel Hawthorne, whose masterpiece The Scarlet Letter remains a seminal study of guilt,
sin, and the rigid morality of Puritan New England. His exploration of the "dark side" of the
human psyche paved the way for the American Gothic tradition.
The mid-19th century witnessed a "literary renaissance" fueled by the transcendentalist
movement. Henry David Thoreau’s Walden advocated for simple living and a deep, spiritual
connection to nature, while Walt Whitman’s Leaves of Grass broke traditional poetic forms with
its expansive free verse, celebrating democracy and the individual. Later, Mark Twain introduced
a new vernacular realism in Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, using humor and regional dialect to
provide a scathing critique of slavery and social hypocrisy. His work signaled a shift away from
European literary models toward a uniquely American voice.
In the 20th century, the "Lost Generation" emerged, disillusioned by the aftermath of World War
I. F. Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby remains the definitive critique of the Jazz Age, capturing
the glitter and hollowness of obsession. Simultaneously, the Harlem Renaissance brought Black
intellectual and artistic life to the forefront; Langston Hughes used the rhythms of jazz and blues
in his poetry to explore the African American experience. Post-war literature saw further
diversification, with Toni Morrison’s Beloved utilizing magical realism to address the harrowing
legacy of slavery.
Today, American literature continues to reflect a multicultural society. Authors like Jhumpa
Lahiri, in The Namesake, explore themes of diaspora, identity, and the immigrant experience.
Ultimately, American literature is a dynamic mirror of a nation in constant flux, utilizing a vast
array of styles to interrogate the complexities of freedom, heritage, and the human condition.
Source: Adapted and revised from The Norton Anthology of American Literature and A Brief
History of American Literature by Richard Gray.

He focused on the celebration of democracy and the individual.
He explored the psychological complexities of guilt and Puritan morality.
He introduced regional dialects to critique social hypocrisy.

SECTION II
Vv.	President Droupadi Murmu on Sunday gave her assent to the ---------(1)--------- , also known as the
VB-G Ram G Act, marking a major shift in India’s rural employment policy. The new legislation
replaces the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), which
was enacted during the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance government and had been in
force for nearly two decades.
According to the Centre, the VB-G Ram G Act introduces significant structural changes while
expanding the legal guarantee of employment in rural areas. One of the key changes is the
increase in the number of guaranteed days of work per household from 100 to 125 days. The
government has positioned this as a step toward strengthening livelihood security for rural
families and improving the quality and impact of public works undertaken under the scheme.
The legislation has, however, drawn criticism from opposition parties and some civil society
groups. Responding to these concerns, Union Minister for wooe---(2)------- Shivraj Singh Chouhan
released a video message defending the new Act. He accused critics of attempting to “mislead” the
public and create “confusion” by portraying the law as a dilution of MGNREGA. Emphasising
continuity rather than dismantling, Mr. Chouhan said the VB-G Ram G Act builds upon and
improves the earlier framework.
Describing the new scheme as “a step forward from MGNREGA,” the Minister highlighted that
provisions related to unemployment allowance have been strengthened. He also pointed out that
the law includes penalties for delays in wage payments, an issue that has frequently affected
workers under the earlier scheme. To support the expanded and restructured programme, the
government has earmarked a budget of 21,51,282 crore, which it says will be used for the
comprehensive development of villages across the country.
A government note explaining the rationale behind the new Act stated that while MGNREGA
primarily focused on the creation of “works,” the VB-G Ram G aims to generate measurable
“outcomes.” Under the new framework, projects will be concentrated in four key areas: water
security, core rural infrastructure, livelihood-related infrastructure, and mitigation of the impacts
of extreme weather events. The Centre will continue as the principal funding partner, following
the 60:40 cost-sharing model used in most centrally sponsored schemes.
Source: The Hindu Article dated 22-4 December, 2025
content.questionText: The acronym VB-G Ram G stands for -
options: Vikasit Bharat - Gram Resource Augmentation Mission (G)uidelines
Village-Based Balanced Growth for Rural Asset Management (G)ram Panchayats
Virasat Bharat - GRam Governance Bill
Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Bill
content.explanation: The relevant fact or inference in the passage corresponds to Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Bill. Therefore option D is the answer identified by the official key.

VI.	The sixth cycle of the All India Tiger Estimation (AITE), popularly known as the tiger census, was
officially launched on Sunday, with ground-level surveys having already begun last month. Union
Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav chaired a high-level joint meeting of the National Tiger
Conservation Authority (NTCA) and the Project Elephant Steering Committee at the Sundarbans
Tiger Reserve. He emphasized that India’s conservation model must increasingly be science-driven
and supported by international collaboration, citing recent delegations from South Africa,
Namibia, and Botswana associated with the cheetah reintroduction programme.
Addressing the growing issue of human—wildlife conflict, Yadav outlined a three-pronged strategy
and announced a specialised initiative titled “Management of Tigers Outside Tiger Reserves.”
Officials also highlighted persistent challenges such as staff shortages, financial limitations, and
the urgent need to control invasive species that threaten wildlife habitats.
On elephant conservation, the Steering Committee reviewed progress on the All-India
Synchronized Elephant Estimation and DNA profiling of captive elephants. Particular focus was
placed on the Nilgiri Elephant Reserve and the Ripu—Chirang Elephant Reserve, along with
renewed attention on assessing elephant corridors and conflict-prone areas in the Bandhavgarh
region. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Following the meeting, Yadav addressed the media on the recent deaths of elephants in a train
collision in Assam’s Hojai district, where seven elephants were killed after being hit by the
Sairang—New Delhi Rajdhani Express, and a calf later died from injuries. The Centre has sought a
detailed report on the incident, and railway authorities have been directed to coordinate closely
with state forest departments to monitor elephant movement along railway tracks. The minister
noted that 1,100 elephant accident-prone zones have been identified across the country, and
district magistrates have been instructed to keep forest officials informed about elephant
movement along highways.
Yadav also disclosed that %112 crore for tiger conservation and %344 crore for elephant-related
projects have been allocated to the Sundarbans over the past five years, though a significant
portion remains unutilised. He compared tourism figures, noting that while the Sundarbans

attract around 9.5 lakh visitors annually, Ranthambore generates 718-19 lakh, stressing the need
for better promotion while maintaining ecological balance.
The meeting ratified several NTCA technical committee decisions, including approval of tiger
conservation plans, expansion of Project Cheetah, tiger translocation, prey-base augmentation,
landscape planning, carnivore health training, and inputs to the National Board for Wildlife.
Updates were shared on expanding Project Cheetah to Gandhisagar Wildlife Sanctuary and
Gujarat’s Banni Grassland. Preparations for a proposed Global Big Cat Summit were reviewed,
and six key publications were released, reinforcing the government’s commitment to a community-
centric conservation approach.
Source: Indian Express article dated 22n¢ December, 2025

content.passageText:
VII. Over the past decade, China and India have shown sharply divergent trajectories in tackling air
pollution. Once infamous for its smog, Beijing reduced its annual PM2.5 levels by more than 50%
between 2013 and 2021, whereas Delhi continues to rank among the world’s most polluted cities.
Beijing’s clean-air transformation resulted from a multifaceted, top-down approach anchored in
coherent policy, strict enforcement, and regional coordination. Key interventions included the Air
Pollution Prevention and Control Action Plan and the Blue Sky Protection Campaign, which
targeted energy, transport, and industry. The government expanded electric mobility, shut down
or relocated polluting industries, replaced coal-fired boilers with natural gas, imposed China VI
vehicular emission standards, and built a dense PM2.5 real-time monitoring system with
substantial penalties for non-compliance. Coordination with neighbouring Tianjin-Hebei provinces
through a unified ‘airshed’ strategy ensured that transboundary pollution was effectively
regulated. These measures drove PM2.5 levels down from 102 pg/m* in 2013 to 31 pg/m* in 2024.
India, by contrast, has a strong statutory framework for environmental protection, including the
Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, the Environment Protection Act, 1986, and
rules covering waste, construction, and emissions. Initiatives such as the National Clean Air
Programme, Graded Response Action Plan, odd-even vehicle rationing, and the Commission for
Air Quality Management (CAQM) exist, yet they are largely reactive and fragmented. Multiple
agencies—from the Union government to municipal bodies—function in silos, slowing decision-
making, weakening enforcement, and diffusing accountability. Pollution control boards are
chronically underfunded and understaffed, and regional coordination, particularly to tackle
stubble burning, remains ineffective.
China’s success also stems from sustained investment in clean energy, electric mobility, and
industrial relocation, whereas Delhi’s attempts, such as the Bawana project and waste-to-energy
plants, have faltered. Delhi’s pollution is compounded by industrial and vehicular emissions,
construction dust, open waste burning, and meteorological inversions. Public transport expansion
and behavioral change have lagged, and temporary measures like odd-even rationing have limited
long-term impact.
For India to achieve meaningful improvement, it need not replicate China’s political system but
can adopt key principles: long-term, mission-oriented governance treating air pollution as a public
health emergency; accelerated clean-energy transition; enforceable transport reforms including
BS-VI compliance, EV infrastructure, and public transport expansion; functional industrial
relocation with monitoring; and regional coordination akin to Beijing’s airshed model for the
Delhi-NCR region.
Source — The Hindu article dated 224 December, 2025

pollution. Once infamous for its smog, Beijing reduced its annual PM2.5 levels by more than 50%
between 2013 and 2021, whereas Delhi continues to rank among the world’s most polluted cities.
Beijing’s clean-air transformation resulted from a multifaceted, top-down approach anchored in
coherent policy, strict enforcement, and regional coordination. Key interventions included the Air
Pollution Prevention and Control Action Plan and the Blue Sky Protection Campaign, which
targeted energy, transport, and industry. The government expanded electric mobility, shut down
or relocated polluting industries, replaced coal-fired boilers with natural gas, imposed China VI
vehicular emission standards, and built a dense PM2.5 real-time monitoring system with
substantial penalties for non-compliance. Coordination with neighbouring Tianjin-Hebei provinces
through a unified ‘airshed’ strategy ensured that transboundary pollution was effectively
regulated. These measures drove PM2.5 levels down from 102 pg/m* in 2013 to 31 pg/m* in 2024.
India, by contrast, has a strong statutory framework for environmental protection, including the
Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, the Environment Protection Act, 1986, and
rules covering waste, construction, and emissions. Initiatives such as the National Clean Air
Programme, Graded Response Action Plan, odd-even vehicle rationing, and the Commission for
Air Quality Management (CAQM) exist, yet they are largely reactive and fragmented. Multiple
agencies—from the Union government to municipal bodies—function in silos, slowing decision-
making, weakening enforcement, and diffusing accountability. Pollution control boards are
chronically underfunded and understaffed, and regional coordination, particularly to tackle
stubble burning, remains ineffective.
China’s success also stems from sustained investment in clean energy, electric mobility, and
industrial relocation, whereas Delhi’s attempts, such as the Bawana project and waste-to-energy
plants, have faltered. Delhi’s pollution is compounded by industrial and vehicular emissions,
construction dust, open waste burning, and meteorological inversions. Public transport expansion
and behavioral change have lagged, and temporary measures like odd-even rationing have limited
long-term impact.
For India to achieve meaningful improvement, it need not replicate China’s political system but
can adopt key principles: long-term, mission-oriented governance treating air pollution as a public
health emergency; accelerated clean-energy transition; enforceable transport reforms including
BS-VI compliance, EV infrastructure, and public transport expansion; functional industrial
relocation with monitoring; and regional coordination akin to Beijing’s airshed model for the
Delhi-NCR region.
Source — The Hindu article dated 224 December, 2025
content.questionText: Why is PM 2.5 considered more dangerous to human health than PM 10?
options: PM 2.5 particles are heavier and settle faster in the air than PM 10.
PM 2.5 can penetrate deeper into the lungs and enter the bloodstream.

PM 10 particles are always more toxic because they contain only industrial chemical
pollutants.
PM 2.5 is only harmful in industrial areas, unlike PM 10.
content.explanation: Particulate matter (PM) is categorized by size, and both PM 10 and PM 2.5 pose significant health risks because they are small enough to be inhaled deep into the respiratory system. The primary difference in their health impact stems from how far they can travel into the body.

content.passageText:
VUI. Sardar Sarovar Dam has been built over the Narmada River in Gujarat. This is one of the largest
water resource projects of India covering four states—Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and
Rajasthan. The Sardar Sarovar project would meet the requirement of water in drought-prone and
desert areas. Sardar Sarovar Project will provide irrigation facilities to 18.45 lakh hectare of land,
covering 3112 villages in 15 districts of Gujarat. It will also irrigate 2,46,000 hectare of land in the
strategic desert districts of Barmer and Jalore in Rajasthan and 37,500 hectare in the tribal hilly
tract of Maharashtra through lift. About 75 per cent of the command area in Gujarat is drought
prone while entire command in Rajasthan is drought prone. Assured water supply will soon make
this area drought proof.
However, in recent years, multi-purpose projects and large dams have come under great scrutiny
and opposition for a variety of reasons. Regulating and damming of rivers affect their natural flow
causing poor sediment flow and excessive sedimentation at the bottom of the reservoir, resulting
in rockier stream beds and poorer habitats for the rivers’ aquatic life. Dams also fragment rivers
making it difficult for aquatic fauna to migrate, especially for spawning. The reservoirs that are
created on the floodplains also submerge the existing vegetation and soil leading to its
decomposition over a period of time.www.lawpreptutorial.com
These floods have not only devastated life and property but also caused extensive soil erosion.
Sedimentation also meant that the flood plains were deprived of silt, a natural fertiliser, further
adding on to the problem of land degradation. It was also observed that the multi purpose projects
induced earthquakes, caused water-borne diseases and pests and pollution resulting from

excessive use of water. Irrigation has also changed the cropping pattern of many regions with
farmers shifting to water intensive and commercial crops. This has great ecological consequences
like salinisation of the soil. Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana has been started which
ensures access to some means to protective irrigation for all agricultural farms in the country,
thus bringing much desired rural prosperity. Some of the broad objectives of this programme are
to enhance the physical access of water on the farm and expand cultivable area under assured
irrigation (har khet ko pani), improve on-farm water use efficiency to reduce wastage and increase
availability both in duration and extent, irrigation and other water saving technologies (per drop
more crop) and introduce sustainable water conservation practices, etc.
Source: NCERT Class X, Contemporary World

water resource projects of India covering four states—Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and

and opposition for a variety of reasons. Regulating and damming of rivers affect their natural flow
causing poor sediment flow and excessive sedimentation at the bottom of the reservoir, resulting
in rockier stream beds and poorer habitats for the rivers’ aquatic life. Dams also fragment rivers
making it difficult for aquatic fauna to migrate, especially for spawning. The reservoirs that are

decomposition over a period of time.www.lawpreptutorial.com

adding on to the problem of land degradation. It was also observed that the multi purpose projects
induced earthquakes, caused water-borne diseases and pests and pollution resulting from

content.passageText:
IX.	The concept of power-sharing has developed as a response to the earlier belief in the concentration
of political power in the hands of a single person or group. Traditionally, it was assumed that
centralized power allowed governments to take quick decisions and enforce them effectively.
Distributing power, it was feared, would weaken authority and slow down governance. However,
with the rise of democratic systems, these ideas have changed significantly. Democracy rests on
the principle that all political power originates from the people. In a democratic setup, citizens
govern themselves through institutions of self-government, and due respect is given to the
diversity of opinions, interests, and social groups present in society. To ensure meaningful
participation and representation, political power must be shared among a wide section of the
population.
Modern democracies adopt various power-sharing arrangements. One important form is the
horizontal distribution of power among the three main organs of government: the legislature,
executive, and judiciary. Although these institutions operate at the same level, they are assigned
different responsibilities and powers. This separation ensures that no single organ can dominate
the others or misuse authority. Each institution acts as a check on the powers of the others,
creating a balance known as the system of checks and balances. For instance, the executive is
accountable to the legislature, while the judiciary can review the actions of both the legislature
and the executive to ensure they follow constitutional principles.
Another significant form of power-sharing is vertical distribution, where authority is divided
among different levels of government. This includes a central or federal government for the entire
country and state or regional governments for different provinces. In India, this system exists
between the Union Government and the State Governments, with the Constitution clearly
defining their respective powers. This principle is also extended to local levels of governance such
as municipalities and panchayats, allowing citizens to participate directly in decision-making at
the grassroots level.
Power can also be shared among different social groups, including religious, linguistic, and ethnic
communities. Such arrangements help ensure fair representation of minorities and socially
weaker sections in governance. Examples include Belgium’s community government and India’s
system of reserved constituencies, which aim to prevent marginalization and foster social
harmony.
Lastly, power-sharing occurs through political parties, pressure groups, and social movements.
Competition among political parties ensures that power does not remain concentrated in one hand.
Coalition governments, formed by alliances of parties, are a direct example of shared power.
Additionally, interest groups influence policymaking by representing various sections of society,
thereby strengthening democratic participation and accountability.
(Source - NCERT Class X, Democratic Politics)

options: Idealism
Federalism
Secularism
Socialism
content.explanation: The relevant fact or inference in the passage corresponds to Federalism. Therefore option B is the answer identified by the official key.

In the context of Article 356 of the Constitution of India, which of the following considerations is
most crucial for determining whether President’s Rule can be validly imposed in a State?

Isolated incidents of disturbance resulting in loss of life and property.

IX.	The concept of power-sharing has developed as a response to the earlier belief in the concentration
of political power in the hands of a single person or group. Traditionally, it was assumed that
centralized power allowed governments to take quick decisions and enforce them effectively.
Distributing power, it was feared, would weaken authority and slow down governance. However,
with the rise of democratic systems, these ideas have changed significantly. Democracy rests on
the principle that all political power originates from the people. In a democratic setup, citizens
govern themselves through institutions of self-government, and due respect is given to the
diversity of opinions, interests, and social groups present in society. To ensure meaningful
participation and representation, political power must be shared among a wide section of the
population.
Modern democracies adopt various power-sharing arrangements. One important form is the
horizontal distribution of power among the three main organs of government: the legislature,
executive, and judiciary. Although these institutions operate at the same level, they are assigned
different responsibilities and powers. This separation ensures that no single organ can dominate
the others or misuse authority. Each institution acts as a check on the powers of the others,
creating a balance known as the system of checks and balances. For instance, the executive is
accountable to the legislature, while the judiciary can review the actions of both the legislature
and the executive to ensure they follow constitutional principles.
Another significant form of power-sharing is vertical distribution, where authority is divided
among different levels of government. This includes a central or federal government for the entire
country and state or regional governments for different provinces. In India, this system exists
between the Union Government and the State Governments, with the Constitution clearly
defining their respective powers. This principle is also extended to local levels of governance such
as municipalities and panchayats, allowing citizens to participate directly in decision-making at
the grassroots level.
Power can also be shared among different social groups, including religious, linguistic, and ethnic
communities. Such arrangements help ensure fair representation of minorities and socially
weaker sections in governance. Examples include Belgium’s community government and India’s
system of reserved constituencies, which aim to prevent marginalization and foster social
harmony.
Lastly, power-sharing occurs through political parties, pressure groups, and social movements.
Competition among political parties ensures that power does not remain concentrated in one hand.
Coalition governments, formed by alliances of parties, are a direct example of shared power.
Additionally, interest groups influence policymaking by representing various sections of society,
thereby strengthening democratic participation and accountability.
(Source - NCERT Class X, Democratic Politics)

XI.	Judicial review signifies the supremacy of law and embodies the authority of courts to examine the
actions of the Legislature, the Executive, and even the Judiciary itself, in order to assess their
conformity with the Constitution. It empowers constitutional courts to scrutinize the validity of
laws, policies, and governmental actions, ensuring that they remain within the bounds prescribed
by the supreme law of the land. Over time, judicial review has evolved into one of the most potent
mechanisms for safeguarding individual liberties in a constitutional democracy and for reinforcing
foundational principles such as the rule of law and the separation of powers. By exercising this
power, the Judiciary acts as a constitutional sentinel, preventing the decisions and actions of other
branches of government from undermining or violating constitutional values. The Constitution, by
its very nature, functions as a document of limitation. Rather than conferring unchecked
authority, it restrains the exercise of power by the State and protects society from the excesses of
majoritarian rule. In this framework, judicial review operates as a protective shield placed in the
hands of constitutional courts, enabling them to preserve the supremacy of the Constitution and to
ensure that democratic governance does not degenerate into arbitrary or unconstitutional exercise
of power. Through this mechanism, courts uphold the delicate balance among the three branches
of government while ensuring that constitutional guarantees remain meaningful and effective.
The scope and contours of judicial review, particularly in relation to legislative enactments, were
elaborated by the Supreme Court in Binoy Viswam v. Union of India & Ors. The Court clarified
that under the Constitution of India, both the Supreme Court and the High Courts are vested with
the authority to review not only executive or administrative actions but also laws enacted by
Parliament and State Legislatures. This power flows from Articles 226, 32, and 136 of the
Constitution, which collectively empower constitutional courts to protect rights and enforce
constitutional limitations. However, the Court emphasized that judicial review of legislative action
operates within narrower parameters when compared to the review of administrative decisions.
While courts undoubtedly possess the power to invalidate legislation, such power is exercised only
on well-defined and limited grounds. Primary legislation may be struck down if it transgresses the
constitutional distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States, or if it violates
fundamental rights or other express provisions of the Constitution. The judiciary’s role as the final
interpreter of the Constitution places it in the position of ultimate arbiter on questions concerning
the existence, scope, and violation of rights.
This authority is firmly rooted in Article 13(2) of the Constitution, which prohibits the State from
enacting any law that abridges or takes away the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part III.
Any law made in contravention of this mandate is rendered void to the extent of such
inconsistency. Judicial review, therefore, serves as the constitutional mechanism through which
this prohibition is enforced, ensuring the continued vitality of fundamental rights and
constitutional supremacy.
Source: Excerpt from the case of Justice K.S.Puttaswamy (Retd) vs Union of India 2018

authority, it restrains the exercise of power by the State and protects society from the excesses of
majoritarian rule. In this framework, judicial review operates as a protective shield placed in the
hands of constitutional courts, enabling them to preserve the supremacy of the Constitution and to
ensure that democratic governance does not degenerate into arbitrary or unconstitutional exercise
of power. Through this mechanism, courts uphold the delicate balance among the three branches
of government while ensuring that constitutional guarantees remain meaningful and effective.
The scope and contours of judicial review, particularly in relation to legislative enactments, were
elaborated by the Supreme Court in Binoy Viswam v. Union of India & Ors. The Court clarified
that under the Constitution of India, both the Supreme Court and the High Courts are vested with
the authority to review not only executive or administrative actions but also laws enacted by
Parliament and State Legislatures. This power flows from Articles 226, 32, and 136 of the
Constitution, which collectively empower constitutional courts to protect rights and enforce
constitutional limitations. However, the Court emphasized that judicial review of legislative action
operates within narrower parameters when compared to the review of administrative decisions.
While courts undoubtedly possess the power to invalidate legislation, such power is exercised only
on well-defined and limited grounds. Primary legislation may be struck down if it transgresses the
constitutional distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States, or if it violates
fundamental rights or other express provisions of the Constitution. The judiciary’s role as the final
interpreter of the Constitution places it in the position of ultimate arbiter on questions concerning
the existence, scope, and violation of rights.
This authority is firmly rooted in Article 13(2) of the Constitution, which prohibits the State from
enacting any law that abridges or takes away the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part III.
Any law made in contravention of this mandate is rendered void to the extent of such
inconsistency. Judicial review, therefore, serves as the constitutional mechanism through which
this prohibition is enforced, ensuring the continued vitality of fundamental rights and
constitutional supremacy.
Source: Excerpt from the case of Justice K.S.Puttaswamy (Retd) vs Union of India 2018

Data showing that 80% of laws passed in the last decade contain technical errors that required

A study showing majorities often bypass debates to pass laws that incrementally erode
minority protections.

XII. In State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu, the Supreme Court of India delivered a
landmark judgment on 8 April 2025, addressing the constitutional limits on the powers of a state
Governor when dealing with bills passed by a state legislature. A two-judge bench held that the
Governor lacks an unfettered veto or “pocket veto” over legislation duly adopted by the State
Assembly and emphasised that the Governor must act in accordance with constitutional
conventions and the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers. The Court observed that prolonged
withholding of assent or referral of bills for presidential consideration undermines democratic
mandates and federal principles. In that context, the bench-imposed timelines directing that
Governors decide on re-enacted bills within one month and on bills reserved for the President
within three months to prevent indefinite delays that can frustrate the legislative will of elected
representatives. Utilizing its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution in the exceptional facts
of the case, the Court also declared ten pending bills as having been effectively assented to, as
they had been stalled for an unreasonable period. The judgment underscored that the Governor’s
actions must respect parliamentary democracy and not impede the functioning of state
legislatures. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Shortly after this ruling, on 13 May 2025, the President of India issued a Presidential Reference
under Article 143(1) of the Constitution to the Supreme Court, seeking its advisory opinion on 14
questions concerning the scope of Governors’ and the President’s powers under Articles 200 and
201, particularly whether the Court could lay down timelines and prescribe how these powers
should be exercised. A five-judge Bench of the Supreme Court on November 20, 2025 answered the
16th Presidential Reference the country has witnessed by opining that the judiciary cannot fetter
Governors and the President to ‘one-size-fits-all’ time-tables to dispose of State Bills or usurp their
functions by assuming ‘deemed consent’ of the proposed laws at the expiry of a court-ordered time
frame. Such a usurpation of the gubernatorial function of the Governor, and similarly of the
President’s functions, is antithetical not only to the spirit of the Constitution, but also specifically,
the doctrine of separation of powers — which is a part of the basic structure of the Constitution,
However, the court clarified that the President and Governors cannot resort to “prolonged and
evasive inaction” by sitting endlessly on State Bills awaiting their approval. This would amount to
a deliberate attempt to thwart the people’s will expressed through the proposed welfare laws
passed by State legislatures.
Source: Excerpt of State Of Tamil Nadu V. Governor of Tamil Nadu (Live Law)
content.questionText:
A State Legislature re-enacts a Bill and sends it back to the Governor. Following the April 8, 2025,
ruling, the Governor fails to act for 45 days. However, the November 20, 2025, Advisory Opinion is
then released. What is the current legal standing of the Governor's delay?
options:
The Bill is automatically deemed effectively assented to because it exceeded the one-month
timeline set in April.

The delay is constitutional because the five-judge bench ruled that the judiciary cannot impose
one-size-fits-all timelines.

The Governor is not bound by a strict one-month deadline but cannot engage in prolonged and
evasive inaction.
The President must now take over the function of the Governor to resolve the deadlock.
content.explanation: This reflects the synthesis of the two rulings. While the November opinion struck down the one-month fixed timetable as a violation of the separation of powers, it explicitly retained the principle that prolonged and evasive inaction is unconstitutional.

content.questionText:
The State Legislature of "Pradesh" passes the Welfare of Farmers Bill in January. The Governor
holds the Bill for four months without comment. In May, the State Assembly re-passes the exact
same Bill and sends it back to the Governor. It is now July (two months later), and the Governor
has still not signed it, claiming he needs more time to study the "federal implications." Based
purely on the Supreme Court’s ruling on April 8, 2025, which of the following is the correct legal
consequence?
options:
The Court can declare the Bill effectively assented to as the Governor exceeded the one-month
timeline for re-enacted bills.

The Governor has the "pocket veto" power to hold the Bill indefinitely if the federal
implications are serious.

The Bill is automatically considered "void" because the Governor did not give assent within the
first month of the initial passing.

The Governor must refer the Bill to the President within three months, and until then, the
Court cannot intervene.
content.explanation: The April Bench rejected the pocket veto, ruling that Governors cannot indefinitely delay bills and must decide on re-enacted legislation within one month. To protect the legislative will, the Court utilized Article 142 to grant "deemed assent" to bills stalled beyond this reasonable period.

In April 2025, the Supreme Court observed that ten welfare bills had been stalled by a Governor
for over two years. Invoking Article 142, which allows the Court to pass any order necessary for
doing complete justice, the bench declared these bills as effectively assented to, bypassing the
requirement for a physical signature from the Governor. In the context of the November 2025
Advisory Opinion, which of the following best describes the constitutional validity of this specific
use of Article 142?
options:
It is constitutionally valid because Article 142 is an overriding power that allows the Court to
ignore the Separation of Powers to achieve complete justice.

It is invalid as the Judiciary cannot usurp the gubernatorial function of granting assent
without violating the Separation of Powers.

It is valid only if the President of India explicitly provides a post-facto confirmation of the
Court’s deemed consent order.

It is invalid because Article 142 can only be used for criminal cases and not for matters
involving state legislation or the Governor’s office.

It held that the Judiciary cannot "usurp" executive functions, as doing so violates the Separation of Powers a part of the Constitution's Basic Structure meaning the Court can command a decision but cannot make it for the Governor.
