content.passageText:
XIII. The status of the Preamble has been one of the most debated subjects in Indian constitutional
jurisprudence, serving as the focal point for defining the relationship between the spirit and the
"letter" of the law. The Preamble to the Constitution of India records the aims and aspirations of
the people, yet its legal enforceability and its status as an integral part of the constitutional
document underwent a significant evolution through two landmark judicial pronouncements. The
first major confrontation with this issue occurred in In Re: Berubari Union (1960). The Supreme
Court was tasked with an advisory opinion regarding the transfer of certain territories to
Pakistan. During the proceedings, the role of the Preamble as a guide to legislative intent was
discussed. The Court acknowledged that the Preamble is a "key to open the mind of the makers"
and shows the general purposes for which they made the several provisions in the Constitution.
However, the Court explicitly held that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution.
Consequently, it was viewed as a decorative introduction that lacked substantive power. The
Court reasoned that since it is not a part of the Constitution, it cannot be regarded as a source of
any substantive power or a limitation on the powers of the government.
This restrictive view remained the law of the land until it was directly challenged and overturned
in the historic case of Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973). A 13-judge Bench the
largest in the history of the Court re-examined the Preamble's status while determining the scope
of Parliament's amending power under Article 368. The Court observed that the history of the
drafting of the Constitution showed that the Preamble was not just an introduction but was
actually voted upon by the Constituent Assembly, unlike the preambles of many other world
constitutions. In a monumental shift, the Supreme Court held that the Preamble is a part of the
Constitution. Justice Sikri observed that the Preamble is of extreme importance and the
Constitution should be read and interpreted in the light of the grand and noble vision expressed in
it. More importantly, the Court held that the Preamble contains the Basic Structure of the
Constitution, which is beyond the amending power of Parliament. While the Preamble itself can be
amended (as it was in 1976), such amendments cannot destroy its fundamental pillars like
secularism, democracy, or socialism.
Source: https://www.legalserviceindia.com /Legal-Articles/preamble-blueprint-of-the-indian-
constitutiona-ideals-and-aspirations /?
content.questionText:
According to the Supreme Court in In Re: Berubari Union, the Preamble was described as a key to
open the mind of the makers. This implies that the Preamble:
options: Has independent legal force
Can override constitutional provisions
Limits Parliament’s constituent power
Assists in understanding legislative intent
content.explanation: As stated in the passage, the Supreme Court in In Re: Berubari Union acknowledged that the Preamble serves as a key to open the mind of the makers, meaning it helps reveal the general purposes and objectives behind the constitutional provisions. However, the Court clarified that this role is purely interpretative, and the Preamble does not possess independent legal force or impose substantive limitations on governmental power.

XIV. A group of former civil servants has expressed serious concern over three recent Supreme Court
decisions related to environmental protection, warning that these rulings signal the growing
influence of “rich and powerful vested interests” over India’s ecological safeguards. In an open
letter dated December 28, the Constitutional Conduct Group (CCG) said it was deeply anguished
that the court, long considered the “last bastion” for environmental protection, appeared to be
setting aside established rules meant to protect the country’s environment. One of the key
decisions criticised is the Supreme Court’s November 20 acceptance of a new, uniform definition of
the Aravalli hill range. Prepared by a committee of eight Union government officials, the
definition restricts the Aravallis to hills rising at least 100 metres above local relief.
Environmentalists argue that this narrower definition could open large parts of the ancient hill
range to commercial activities, particularly mining. The CCG echoed these fears, warning that
such activities would weaken the Aravallis’ role as a dust barrier for Delhi, accelerate
desertification, destroy habitats, fragment ecosystems, and undermine the hills’ function as an
aquifer. The group also cautioned that increased mining would worsen already severe air pollution
in Delhi-NCR, disproportionately harming marginalised communities who work outdoors and lack
access to protective measures such as air purifiers. The Supreme Court has since taken suo motu
cognisance of the controversy and is scheduled to hear the matter. The second decision highlighted
by the CCG is the court’s November 18 order recalling its earlier May ruling, which had declared
post-facto environmental clearances for construction projects to be a “gross illegality’. While the

matter is now to be decided by a larger bench, the group urged the court to restore its earlier
stance, especially in light of worsening climate extremes and record levels of air pollution in north
India. The third concern relates to the Supreme Court’s November 22 decision preventing the
government from disbanding the Central Empowered Committee (CEC) without court approval.
The CEC, established in 2002 to monitor compliance with court orders on forests and wildlife, is
alleged by the CCG to have lost its independence and come under the influence of the Union
environment ministry. The group pointed out that a CEC official was part of the committee that
drafted the new Aravalli definition and reiterated earlier concerns about the removal of
independent members from the committee. In conclusion, the CCG warned that these decisions,
taken in quick succession, threaten both environmental conservation and citizens’ right to life. The
group urged the Supreme Court to prioritise public health over corporate interests and to uphold
established principles such as “polluter pays”, the precautionary principle, and intergenerational
equity.
Source: The Wire dated article 29 December 2025
content.questionText:
The Supreme Court accepted a new, uniform definition of the Aravalli hill range, restricting it to
hills rising at least 100 metres above local relief. This definition was prepared by a committee of
Union government officials. Environmental groups argue that the revised definition could allow
mining and commercial activities in large parts of the Aravallis, thereby weakening its role as a
dust barrier for Delhi, accelerating desertification, destroying habitats, fragmenting ecosystems,
and damaging groundwater recharge. A group of environmental organisations and residents files a
petition challenging the decision, claiming that it violates their right to life under Article 21.
Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action the petitioners can seek from the
Supreme Court, in line with established environmental jurisprudence?
options:
Direct the immediate implementation of the new definition while leaving environmental
protection entirely to future executive regulations.

Stay the new definition and appoint an independent committee to assess impact using the
precautionary principle.

Dismiss the petition on the ground that environmental policy falls exclusively within the
domain of the executive.

Allow mining activities to continue under the new definition, subject only to higher financial
penalties for violations.
content.explanation: Option B aligns with Article 21 and the precautionary principle, allowing judicial intervention to prevent potential irreversible environmental harm. The other options either avoid judicial scrutiny or permit environmental damage to occur before safeguards are assessed.

evidence.explanation: Option B aligns with Article 21 and the precautionary principle, allowing judicial intervention to prevent potential irreversible environmental harm. The other options either avoid judicial scrutiny or permit environmental damage to occur before safeguards are assessed.

XV. Amid loud protests from the opposition, the Karnataka Legislative Assembly on December 18
passed the Karnataka Hate Speech and Hate Crimes (Prevention) Bill, 2025, in Belagavi. The
legislation prescribes imprisonment of one to seven years along with fines for hate crimes. For
repeat offences, imprisonment ranges from two to seven years with higher fines. The Bill covers
communication made in public through verbal, print, public, or electronic means.

XV. Amid loud protests from the opposition, the Karnataka Legislative Assembly on December 18
passed the Karnataka Hate Speech and Hate Crimes (Prevention) Bill, 2025, in Belagavi. The
legislation prescribes imprisonment of one to seven years along with fines for hate crimes. For
repeat offences, imprisonment ranges from two to seven years with higher fines. The Bill covers
communication made in public through verbal, print, public, or electronic means.
While tabling the Bill, Home Minister G. Parameshwara cited a Supreme Court ruling delivered
on May 5 this year, which emphasised the need for firm action against communal hate. He noted
that hate speech had led to killings and inter-community violence, harming social harmony. The
legislation aims to protect constitutional values by addressing discrimination rooted in religion,
race, caste, gender, language, and other identities. According to Parameshwara, the objective is to
curb and prevent dissemination, publication, or promotion of hate speech that causes disharmony
or hatred against a person or group. The home minister explained that existing preventive
restrictions on provocative speech were insufficient. Alerts about potential inflammatory speech
could lead to temporary bans, but this was not a long-term solution. Therefore, a separate law was

required, as provocative speeches were often followed by violent incidents. The government is
authorised to direct the removal of hate speech material from media platforms. Hate crime under
the Bill is defined as communicating or promoting hate speech to cause disharmony, enmity, or ill-
will against individuals or groups.
The Bill makes hate speech a cognizable, non-bailable offence, and offenders can be tried by a
Judicial Magistrate First Class. For organisations, persons in charge at the time of the offence are
deemed liable.
The Congress government-initiated discussions on a hate speech law in June after a series of
communal killings in coastal Karnataka, beginning with the lynching of a Muslim man, Ashraf, in
April. Leader of the opposition R. Ashok opposed the Bill, tearing a copy in the assembly and
claiming it infringed on Article 19(1), which guarantees free expression. He argued that police
could misuse the law for political purposes, targeting journalists and opposition members. Ashok
suggested existing provisions in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita were adequate. The debate
intensified after Urban Development Minister Byrathi Suresh made a remark directed at BJP
MLA Vedavyas Kamath, prompting the opposition to demand its removal from the official record.
Despite protests, Parameshwara appealed for support, and the speaker announced the Bill had
been approved through a voice vote before adjourning the House for lunch. BJP MLAs later stated
they were caught off guard by the passage without full debate. Minister for Law H.K. Patil
emphasised that the Bill had been passed and could not be discussed again. The Bill seeks to
address communal disharmony by making hate speech and hate crimes punishable under clear
statutory provisions, ensuring swift action against offenders and promoting social harmony in
Karnataka.
Source: The Wire dated Article 19» December 2025

content.passageText:
XVII. The recent nationwide strike by a vast cohort of gig workers has exposed the precariousness
embedded within India’s emerging labour framework for platform-mediated work. This unrest
unfolded immediately after the Labour Ministry released draft Rules to operationalise the revised
labour codes, highlighting a fundamental disjunction between regulatory intent and lived labour
realities. While these Rules formally acknowledge gig workers within the social security
architecture, they conspicuously exclude them from statutory protections relating to wages and
working conditions. By severing gig work from the traditional employment relationship for wage
determination, the framework relegates platforms to the limited obligation of making aggregate
contributions to a social security fund, leaving core worker grievances unresolved. The Code on
Wages, though ostensibly universal, exempts gig workers by categorising their labour as distinct
from employment, thereby permitting algorithmic rate reductions and opaque incentive
mechanisms to persist unchecked. Similarly, the Occupational Safety, Health and Working
Conditions Rules adopt a compliance-centric model predicated on employer reporting via the
Shram Suvidha Portal — an approach ill-suited to the dispersed, app-mediated nature of gig
labour. In effect, social security emerges as the sole substantive reform, yet even here, access
remains contingent and procedurally burdensome. Under the draft provisions, gig workers must
register on a designated portal, while aggregators are required to periodically upload engagement
data. Eligibility hinges on minimum thresholds of 90 days with a single platform or 120
cumulative days across platforms within a financial year. Although multiple engagements within
a single day may be counted multiplicatively, this technical accommodation fails to constrain
platform control over work allocation. More critically, such temporal thresholds risk penalising
workers engaged in unpaid care labour, suffering illness, maternity-related interruptions, or
facing demand volatility beyond their control.

Consequently, the draft Rules necessitate substantive redesign to ensure that social security is not
merely nominal but operationally meaningful. Threshold criteria must incorporate explicit
safeguards against involuntary work discontinuities and prevent lapses arising from transient
downturns. Furthermore, the framework must delineate the specific benefits available, prescribe
minimum entitlements supported by the Social Security Fund, and establish a transparent, time-
bound mechanism for claims, grievances, and appeals independent of platform discretion. Finally,
procedural transparency must be institutionalised. Aggregators should be mandated to furnish
workers with regular statements detailing tasks completed, hours logged, earnings accrued, and
deductions imposed, alongside a robust mechanism for contesting inaccuracies. Absent such
reforms, the proposed regime risks entrenching the very structural insecurity that precipitated
collective action among gig workers, rendering regulatory recognition hollow rather than
transformative.
content.questionText: Which of the following can be most reasonably inferred from the passage?
options: The new labour codes intentionally weaken protections for gig workers
Formal recognition of gig workers does not guarantee real protection.
Social security reforms alone are sufficient to stabilise gig work
Platform companies are legally incapable of ensuring worker welfare
content.explanation: This question tests whether you can distinguish recognition from protection. The passage repeatedly argues that while gig workers are formally included in social security, the protections are procedural, partial, and fragile.

XVIII. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization, one-third of food produced for human
consumption is lost or wasted globally. Food is lost or wasted throughout the supply chain, from
initial agricultural production to final household consumption. The increasing wastage also results
in land degradation by about 45%, mainly due to deforestation, unsustainable agricultural
practices, and excessive groundwater extraction. The energy spent over wasted food results in
about 3-5 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide production every year. Decay also leads to harmful
emissions of other gases in the atmosphere. Addressing the loss and wastage of food in all forms is
critical to complete the cycle of food sufficiency and food sustainability.

SECTION I
L	“Last night she came to me again.”
In the dream, they were girls once more, sitting on opposite beds, their legs not touching the
marble floor. Damla’s braid fell thick against her shoulder. “We hadn’t aged at all,” the narrator
recalls. But this time Damla had returned “to tell me something.” That summer had begun
without ceremony. “We'll take her,” the father had said in the dark house in the hills. “The girls
will sleep in one room. They’re basically sisters.” Damla did not look up. There was bitter tea,
wrapped sweets, and a silence that felt heavier than words. The village lay open toward the sea—
“like the world opening up.” Boats rolled down the sand in bright colors, and the two girls took
refuge in the cabin of Penelope. Captain would find them crouched inside cabinets. “Girls, girls,
girls,” he laughed once. “What're you doing here again, with all the ghosts?” “Do you think it’s
true?” Damla asked afterward. “We'll wait here and see if they come,” she said. They summoned
names they barely understood. “Melike,” Damla whispered into a shell pressed to the floor of the
rocking cabin. “We want to talk to you.” The shell slid across the wood. Pebbles swished outside.
At night, beneath a ceiling fan and mosquito net, they lay on their backs. “She died, but she didn’t
leave,” the narrator said of Melike. “Did you ever see her afterward?” Damla asked. “No.” They
were fearless together. “We owned the world with our stories.” They imagined ropes loosening,
sails speaking, the sea answering back. They did not imagine consequence. One afternoon they
saw Uncle laughing with Captain. Damla shrank. “Are they friends, then?” she asked quietly. The
narrator shrugged. “Does he ever ask about me?” Damla pressed. “Yes,” she said. “Sometimes.” It
might not have been true. The next day they untied the “sturdiest knots,” impatient for something
to happen—for the ghost to come. Nothing was said when Captain climbed the mast. They
watched from below. “We might have stepped forward to warn him about the ropes,” the narrator
admits. They were forming the words. Waiting. There was a moment—just before he fell—“that he
floated in the air.” Years later, the narrator hears that there is a poster of Damla in the
coffeehouse. She has not returned to the village. She remembers only the summer when they
believed themselves “irrelevant as ghosts,” and wonders what they truly disturbed.
Source: Story: “Ghosts” by Aysegitil Savas, extracted from literary hub

content.passageText:
I.	Few puzzles expose the limits of human intuition as sharply as the Monty Hall Problem. The
scenario is deceptively simple: three doors, one car, two goats. You select a door. The host—who
knows where the car is—opens another door, deliberately revealing a goat. You are then offered a
choice: stay with your original selection or switch.
Most people instinctively reason that once a goat has been revealed, only two doors remain, and
therefore the odds must be evenly split. The situation appears symmetrical. Two unopened doors.
One prize. A 50/50 gamble.
But symmetry here is an illusion.
Your initial choice had only a one-in-three chance of being correct. The remaining two doors
collectively held a two-in-three probability of hiding the car. When the host opens a goat door—
crucially, one he knows to be empty—he is not redistributing probability. He is revealing
information. The entire two-in-three likelihood collapses onto the single unopened alternative.
Staying preserves your original one-in-three odds. Switching transfers you to the two-in-three
probability you initially rejected.
For those who find this explanation unconvincing, expanding the problem clarifies the logic.
Imagine 100 doors instead of three. You choose one. The host opens 98 others, each containing
goats. Two doors remain: yours and one other. It now feels far less plausible that your original
pick—made when the odds were one in one hundred—should suddenly become equally likely.
Yet resistance to this reasoning is remarkably common. When the correct solution was published
in a widely read column in 1990, thousands of readers insisted it was wrong. Even mathematically
trained individuals struggled to accept it. The discomfort reveals something important: human
reasoning is deeply shaped by surface appearance rather than probabilistic structure.
The Monty Hall Problem is not merely about doors and goats. It is about how easily intuition can
mislead us—and how reluctantly we surrender it, even when confronted with proof.
Source: Adapted from a widely discussed probability puzzle known as The Monty Hall Problem,
originally popularized in 1990 through Marilyn vos Savant’s Ask Marilyn column in Parade
magazine.

Industry” does not operate only at the level of tourism; it thrives equally in high culture.
Biographies, adaptations, films, academic conferences, and critical studies have multiplied to the
point where the words written about Kafka vastly exceed those written by him.
This construction of Kafka began early. Max Brod, who preserved and published his friend’s
manuscripts, also fashioned an image of Kafka as a saintly seer—an allegorical prophet whose
works were to be decoded across generations. Later commentators extended this portrait. What
emerged was not merely Kafka the writer, but Kafka the symbol. Milan Kundera later criticized
what he called “Kafkology,” arguing that critics often replaced Kafka with a “Kafkologized Kafka,”

at a time of rising nationalism and anti-Semitism. His city was transforming; the old Jewish
quarter was demolished, and violence periodically erupted. Under Communist rule his works were
banned for “decadent anti-realism,” only to be reclaimed during the Prague Spring. Each political
regime seemed to discover its own Kafka.

Agnieszka Holland’s film Franz presents a restrained portrait of Kafka as a private man rather
than a prophet. Yet the very act of producing another film contributes to what it seeks to resist.

no image of Gregor’s transformed body appear on the cover. He resisted easy visualization and
feared that interpretation would smother the work. But denial invites curiosity. The result is a
paradox: it feels impossible to write anything new about Kafka, and yet impossible not to write
about him.

commercialize, and canonize. The industry continues to grow—even this essay becomes part of it.

content.passageText:
IV.	They tell her she can be rewritten. They say she can be pressed into the margins of history,
distorted by “twisted lies,” ” dragged through dust, stamped into the ground until nothing
recognizable remains. She hears them. She does not pretend the voices are absent. But like dust—
restless, inevitable, rising at the slightest disturbance—she rises.
Their objections turn personal. Why is she so confident? Why does she laugh as though she owns
the room? Why does her presence feel like possession? She smiles at the accusation and answers
without apology: “Because I do.” Not with gold, not with property, but with dignity stored deep in
the marrow. She walks as though abundance runs beneath her feet, as though worth is not
granted but inherent.
They warn her she will not survive. They threaten silence. They promise words sharp enough to
cut bone. The intention is clear: diminish, contain, erase. Yet the answer remains unchanged.
Still—she rises.
Her rising does not begin with her. It stands on backs bent under chains, on hands hardened by
labor, on grief swallowed so children might eat. “I carried bricks until my back broke,” one voice
says. “I swallowed grief,” another echoes. The weight of history presses forward, but she refuses to
crouch beneath it. She acknowledges where she comes from. She will not kneel there.
They command her to shrink. To stay in her place. To bend. But her ascent moves like the moon
drawing tides, like the sun insisting on morning. It obeys a law older than cruelty. When they
demand to know why she does not break, she answers simply: resilience is elemental. It is not
borrowed. It is born.
The “I” she speaks is no longer solitary. It gathers mothers, daughters, unnamed spirits—those
told they were too dark, too loud, too much; those told they were nothing at all. The rising becomes
plural. It becomes shared. It becomes luminous.
She does not request permission. She does not bargain for worth. She names herself “the dream
and the hope of those who endured the unendurable.” And when the final question comes—“And
you?”—she answers without hesitation.
“T rise.”
And still—she rises.
Source: Inspired by “Still I Rise” — Maya Angelou
(Adapted into unified prose for examination use)

content.passageText:
V.	Childhood does not need to be engineered in order to be meaningful. It does not require constant
supervision, performance tracking, or carefully curated enrichment. In fact, much of what forms a
durable human being cannot be scheduled at all.
A sandpile can do what expensive playgrounds cannot. A river can replace structured
entertainment. When children are given space rather than instruction, imagination does not
decline; it intensifies. Castles rise from handfuls of sand. Worlds are built without manuals. In
such freedom, attention deepens and creativity becomes habitual rather than assigned.
Yet play alone is not enough. Children also need responsibility. Water must be carried. Wood must
be split. Grass must be cut even when the sun is high and the work is tedious. Chores are not
punishments; they are invitations into contribution. Through repetition and effort, endurance
forms quietly. Resentment fades. Capacity grows.
There is a difference between stretching a child and overmanaging one. Intellectual stimulation
matters, but it cannot replace discipline. A résumé may record achievements, but it does not
measure perseverance. When every hour is organized and optimized, children risk becoming
performers rather than participants in life.
Love, too, must sometimes yield to responsibility. To hold tightly to what we enjoy, even when it
harms others, is immaturity disguised as affection. To let go when necessary is painful—but
formative.
The task of parenting, then, is not to accelerate adulthood. It is to preserve wonder while
cultivating steadiness. It is to resist the urge to produce brilliance at the cost of resilience. A child
does not need to be constantly improved. A child needs room to imagine, work to do, and adults
humble enough to step down from their ambitions long enough to see the world at eye level.
Source: Adapted from Johann Christoph Arnold, “Sandpile Parenting”, Plough Quarterly

VI.	The India-United Arab Emirates (UAE) Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA)
is completing three years of its signing on 18th February 2025. CEPA is a full and deep Agreement
which was signed on 18th February 2022, during a virtual summit between the Hon’ble Prime
Minister of India, Shri Narendra Modi and His Excellency the President of the UAE and Ruler of
Abu Dhabi, His Highness (1). It entered into force from 01st May 2022.
Since the signing of CEPA, bilateral merchandise trade has nearly doubled from USD 43.3 billion
in FY 2020-21 to USD 83.7 billion in 2023-24. During the current FY till January’25, it reached
USD 80.5 billion. CEPA has been successful in realising its potential of diversification of trade
basket as non-oil trade touched USD 57.8 billion in FY 2023-24 accounting for more than half of
the total trade. This is attuned to the target of taking bilateral non-oil trade to USD 100 billion
level by 2030. In terms of utilization of CEPA preferential duties are concerned, since coming into
force, nearly 2,40,000 Certificates of Origin have been issued against which total export of USD
19.87 billion have been made to the UAE.
In terms of India’s exports, non-oil exports reached USD 27.4 billion in FY 2023-24 recording an
average growth of 25.6% since entering into force of CEPA at the sectoral level, besides refined
crude oil products and gems & jewellery products, electrical machinery and equipment, light &
medium high technology goods like boilers, generators and reactors and organic & in-organic
chemicals have been major achievers. Besides, at the product level, smartphones have emerged as
a major item of export with shipments valued USD 2.57 billion bound for the UAE during FY 2023-
24.
Source: https://www.pi(b)gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx? PRID=21 04450&reg=s3&lang=2

community, largely residing in the Imphal Valley, and the Kuki-Zo tribal groups inhabiting the
hill districts. What began as tensions over identity and constitutional protections escalated into

action benefits, affect land ownership rights in the hills, and weaken their political representation.

and led to widespread unrest.

displacement of nearly 60,000 people. Many displaced individuals continue to reside in relief
camps. The crisis was marked by repeated curfews, extended internet shutdowns, and persistent
instability, which effectively segregated communities and disrupted normal life across large parts
of Manipur.

his inability to restore peace. Political instability intensified, and on February 9, 2025, after nearly
20 months of violence and amid the threat of a no-confidence motion in the Manipur Legislative
Assembly, he resigned Following this, President’s Rule was imposed, indicating a breakdown of
constitutional governance in the state.

MLAs, including seven from the Kuki-Zo community. In early 2026, efforts to restore an elected
government gained momentum. On February 2, 2026, the BJP appointed Tarun Chugh as central
observer to oversee the election of its Legislature Party leader. The next day, Yumnam
Khemchand Singh was elected leader, paving the way for his appointment as Chief Minister.

VIII. Saina Nehwal’s quiet acknowledgement of retirement, shared casually on a podcast rather than
through a formal announcement, was met with a muted response. Having been away from
competitive badminton for nearly two years, her absence had already begun to feel inevitable—
another familiar story of time, injuries, and the slow fading of an athlete from the circuit. Saina
herself seemed unconcerned with ceremony, remarking that she entered and exited the sport on
her own terms, and therefore saw no need to officially declare her retirement. Yet, regardless of
her personal nonchalance, the history of Indian sport cannot afford to treat her departure so
lightly.
The initial sense of ennui quickly gave way to reflection. Once the reality of her exit settled in,
reassessment and retrospection followed Saina Nehwal is not merely a former world No. 1 or an
accomplished shuttler whose career statistics can be neatly archived She represents a turning
point—an athlete whose influence reshaped the sporting landscape of an entire nation.
Before Saina, badminton in India existed largely on the fringes of mainstream sporting
consciousness. It did not command packed stadiums, sustained television coverage, or the
aspirations of thousands of young athletes, especially girls. The sport lacked visible role models
who could convincingly challenge the dominance of traditional powerhouses like China and
Europe. Saina changed that narrative through sheer persistence, ambition, and excellence. Her
rise was not just personal success; it was symbolic defiance against an established global order.

What distinguishes Saina’s legacy is not limited to medals, rankings, or podium finishes, though
those were significant. Her true contribution lies in the irreversible shift she triggered in Indian
badminton. She made the sport aspirational. Young girls across the country, many from modest
backgrounds, suddenly saw a viable professional future with a racquet in hand Parents, coaches,
sponsors, and administrators began to take badminton seriously, investing time, money, and belief
into a system that previously lacked confidence.
Saina’s journey was defined by grit—years of grinding on practice courts, pushing her physical
limits, and enduring injuries that ultimately took their toll. Yet even as her body began to recede
from elite competition, her impact continued to expand She became proof that Indian athletes
could not only compete but dominate on the world stage in individual sports traditionally
monopolized by other nations.
Though she may choose to frame her exit as casual and unremarkable, history will not. Saina
Nehwal will endure in Indian sporting memory not just as a champion, but as a catalyst—someone
who transformed badminton from a niche pursuit into a national conversation, and whose
influence will echo through generations of players who followed the path she carved

IX.	The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, initially emerged as a platform for dialogue
between educated Indian elites and the British colonial administration. In its early phase, the
Congress relied on constitutional methods such as petitions, resolutions, and appeals, reflecting
the belief that political progress could be achieved through gradual reforms within the colonial
framework. This approach was shaped by the socio-political context of the time, where mass
political mobilization was neither feasible nor widely accepted
However, the limitations of this moderate strategy became increasingly evident in the early
twentieth century. The failure of the British government to respond meaningfully to Indian
demands, combined with economic hardships and racial discrimination, led to growing
disillusionment among nationalist leaders. As a result, the Congress gradually transformed its

methods and objectives, incorporating mass participation and more assertive forms of protest. This
shift marked a significant change in the nature of the nationalist movement—from elite
negotiation to popular mobilization.
The entry of Mahatma Gandhi into the Congress further altered its character. By emphasizing
non-violence and mass participation, Gandhi enabled the Congress to reach peasants, workers, and
marginalized groups, thereby broadening its social base. Movements such as Non-Cooperation and
Civil Disobedience reflected this new strategy, which sought to challenge colonial authority by
undermining its moral and administrative legitimacy rather than relying solely on constitutional
agitation.
Despite internal disagreements and periodic setbacks, the Congress remained the central force of
the Indian freedom struggle. Its ability to adapt to changing political circumstances, balance
ideological differences, and integrate diverse social interests allowed it to sustain relevance over
decades. The evolution of the Indian National Congress thus illustrates how nationalist
movements often reshape their strategies in response to political realities, rather than following a
fixed ideological path.
Source: Themes in Indian History — Part II “Colonialism and the Countryside / The Nationalist
Movement”)

X.	The Union Budget 2026-27 places strong emphasis on expenditure programmes aimed at
achieving the goal of a developed India by (1). The Finance Minister highlighted investments in
advanced technology sectors such as artificial intelligence, biopharma, semiconductors, and critical
minerals. While this focus is appropriate for long-term growth, concerns remain regarding the
effectiveness of implementation and the speed at which these initiatives can translate into tangible
outcomes.
To create fiscal space for these priorities, the Government of India has restructured its expenditure
pattern over the past decade. The share of revenue expenditure in total expenditure has declined
significantly from 88% in 2014-15 to about 77% in 2026-27 (BE), a reduction of 11 percentage
points. A major contributor to this decline has been a reduction in central subsidies, which fell by
about 7 percentage points. Correspondingly, the share of capital expenditure has increased,
reflecting the government’s intent to promote growth through infrastructure and asset creation.
Capital expenditure has played a key role in supporting GDP growth, particularly in the post-
COVID period, when it remained high as a percentage of GDP. However, its growth rate has
steadily declined—from 28.3% in 2023-24 to 10.8% in 2024-25 and further to 4.2% in 2025-26
(RE). Although capital expenditure is budgeted to grow by 11.5% in 2026-27, this is only
marginally higher than the projected nominal GDP growth of 10%, implying that capital
expenditure will remain almost stagnant at around 3.1% of GDP.
On the revenue side, tax projections for 2026-27 appear cautious and achievable. Nevertheless, the
buoyancy of gross tax revenues has fallen to 0.8, below the desirable benchmark of 1. While direct
taxes show reasonable buoyancy at 1.1, indirect taxes lag significantly at 0.3, mainly due to slower
growth in GST collections. Given rising developmental and welfare expenditure pressures,
improving indirect tax buoyancy is crucial.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Finally, the Sixteenth Finance Commission has retained the States’ share in the divisible pool at
41% but discontinued revenue deficit grants and reduced overall Finance Commission grants. As a
result, total transfers to States have declined, marking a departure from the usual increase seen at
the start of a new Finance Commission cycle.

achieving the goal of a developed India by (1). The Finance Minister highlighted investments in

minerals. While this focus is appropriate for long-term growth, concerns remain regarding the

outcomes.

pattern over the past decade. The share of revenue expenditure in total expenditure has declined
significantly from 88% in 2014-15 to about 77% in 2026-27 (BE), a reduction of 11 percentage
points. A major contributor to this decline has been a reduction in central subsidies, which fell by
about 7 percentage points. Correspondingly, the share of capital expenditure has increased,
reflecting the government’s intent to promote growth through infrastructure and asset creation.
Capital expenditure has played a key role in supporting GDP growth, particularly in the post-
COVID period, when it remained high as a percentage of GDP. However, its growth rate has
steadily declined—from 28.3% in 2023-24 to 10.8% in 2024-25 and further to 4.2% in 2025-26
(RE). Although capital expenditure is budgeted to grow by 11.5% in 2026-27, this is only
marginally higher than the projected nominal GDP growth of 10%, implying that capital
expenditure will remain almost stagnant at around 3.1% of GDP.

buoyancy of gross tax revenues has fallen to 0.8, below the desirable benchmark of 1. While direct
taxes show reasonable buoyancy at 1.1, indirect taxes lag significantly at 0.3, mainly due to slower
growth in GST collections. Given rising developmental and welfare expenditure pressures,
improving indirect tax buoyancy is crucial.www.lawpreptutorial.com

XI.	The United States and India have announced a framework for an Interim Agreement on reciprocal
and mutually beneficial trade. This agreement marks a significant step in strengthening economic
ties between the two countries and reinforces their commitment to the broader U.S.-India Bilateral
Trade Agreement (BTA) negotiations. The BTA talks were launched on February 13, 2025, by
President Donald J. Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The Interim Agreement is
described as a historic milestone that reflects a shared commitment to balanced and reciprocal
trade based on mutual interests and tangible outcomes.
The Interim Agreement lays the groundwork for deeper economic cooperation and aims to support
more resilient and diversified supply chains. It also seeks to address trade imbalances while
expanding market access opportunities for businesses in both countries.
Under the key terms of the framework, India has agreed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on all U.S.
industrial goods. In addition, it will lower duties on a wide range of U.S. food and agricultural
products. These include dried distillers’ grains (DDGs), red sorghum used for animal feed, tree
nuts, fresh and processed fruits, soybean oil, wine and spirits, and other agricultural commodities.
This move is expected to provide significant market access for American exporters and enhance
agricultural trade between the two nations.
On the other side, the United States will apply a reciprocal tariff rate of 18 percent on originating
goods from India under Executive Order 14257, issued on April 2, 2025. This order was designed to
regulate imports with a reciprocal tariff to address trade practices contributing to large and
persistent U.S. goods trade deficits. The 18 percent tariff will apply to a range of Indian exports,
including textiles and apparel, leather and footwear, plastic and rubber products, organic
chemicals, home décor, artisanal goods, and certain machinery.
However, the agreement also provides for the removal of reciprocal tariffs on a broad set of goods,
subject to the successful conclusion of the Interim Agreement. According to the Potential Tariff
Adjustments for Aligned Partners Annex under Executive Order 14346 of September 5, 2025, the
United States will eliminate tariffs on products such as generic pharmaceuticals, gems and
diamonds, and aircraft parts. These adjustments aim to promote aligned trade partnerships and
facilitate smoother trade flows in key sectors.
Overall, the Interim Agreement represents a strategic effort by both countries to deepen trade
relations, promote fairness, and create a more predictable and cooperative economic framework. It
sets the stage for further negotiations under the broader Bilateral Trade Agreement while
delivering immediate trade benefits and reinforcing the long-term partnership between the United
States and India

SECTION III
XII. The Supreme Court has overturned the Allahabad high court’s observation that assaulting a
minor by grabbing her breasts and attempting to disrobe her did not amount to attempted rape,
and has directed the formation of a panel to draft sensitivity guidelines for judges handling sexual
offence cases.
On February 10, 2026 the Supreme Court set aside the Allahabad High Court's March 17, 2025
order that had controversially held that the acts of grabbing a child’s breasts, breaking her pyjama
string, and attempting to drag her under a culvert did not amount to rape or attempted rape.
A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and NV Anjaria ruled that such acts
clearly constituted attempted rape/penetrative sexual assault under the POCSO Act, rejecting the
high court's view that they were merely “preparatory.”
"We cannot agree with the finding of the high court that the allegations only amount to
preparation, but not an attempt, towards the commission of the offence of rape,” the SC bench
ruled.
Further, the bench emphasised that adjudication in sexual offence cases must be rooted in law and
empathy, cautioning that justice cannot be delivered if courts are “inconsiderate” to victims’
vulnerabilities.
In its judgment delivered on February 10, the bench cautioned that courts cannot deliver
“complete justice” if they are “inconsiderate” to the vulnerabilities of litigants.
"The court's decisions must reflect the ethos of compassion, humanity, and understanding, which
are essential for creating a fair and effective justice system,’ the bench said.
It stressed the need for systemic correction and greater sensitivity among judges, noting that
judicial decisions must reflect compassion, humanity, and understanding. Training and guidelines
are required to nurture sensitivity in handling sexual offence cases.
The Allahabad High Court had made the controversial observations on March 17, 2025, while
modifying a summoning order against two accused persons. According to the prosecution, the
accused, Pawan and Akash, allegedly assaulted an 11-year-old girl, grabbing her breasts, breaking
her pyjama string, and trying to drag her beneath a culvert. However, they fled after passers-by
intervened.
The trial court charged them under Section 376 IPC (rape) and Section 18 POCSO (attempt). The
high court, however, reduced charges to Section 354-B IPC (assault with intent to disrobe) and
Sections 9/10 POCSO (aggravated sexual assault), stating there was no “determined intent” to
commit rape.
The SC later took suo motu cognizance of the order and stayed it on March 26, 2025. However, it
declined to frame any immediate guidelines itself, citing the need for a comprehensive study.
The SC has now directed the National Judicial Academy (NJA), Bhopal to form a committee of
experts to draft guidelines to inculcate "sensitivity and compassion" in judges and judicial
processes in cases of sexual offences.
The SC also stressed that the guidelines must be in simple, accessible language, avoiding complex
foreign expressions, and asked the NJA to submit its report preferably within three months.
Source: https://thefederal.com/category /news/sc-overturns-allahabad-hc-controversial-order-
child-assault-case-judicial-empathy-230406

SECTION III
XII. The Supreme Court has overturned the Allahabad high court’s observation that assaulting a
minor by grabbing her breasts and attempting to disrobe her did not amount to attempted rape,
and has directed the formation of a panel to draft sensitivity guidelines for judges handling sexual
offence cases.
On February 10, 2026 the Supreme Court set aside the Allahabad High Court's March 17, 2025
order that had controversially held that the acts of grabbing a child’s breasts, breaking her pyjama
string, and attempting to drag her under a culvert did not amount to rape or attempted rape.
A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and NV Anjaria ruled that such acts
clearly constituted attempted rape/penetrative sexual assault under the POCSO Act, rejecting the
high court's view that they were merely “preparatory.”
"We cannot agree with the finding of the high court that the allegations only amount to
preparation, but not an attempt, towards the commission of the offence of rape,” the SC bench
ruled.
Further, the bench emphasised that adjudication in sexual offence cases must be rooted in law and
empathy, cautioning that justice cannot be delivered if courts are “inconsiderate” to victims’
vulnerabilities.
In its judgment delivered on February 10, the bench cautioned that courts cannot deliver
“complete justice” if they are “inconsiderate” to the vulnerabilities of litigants.
"The court's decisions must reflect the ethos of compassion, humanity, and understanding, which
are essential for creating a fair and effective justice system,’ the bench said.
It stressed the need for systemic correction and greater sensitivity among judges, noting that
judicial decisions must reflect compassion, humanity, and understanding. Training and guidelines
are required to nurture sensitivity in handling sexual offence cases.
The Allahabad High Court had made the controversial observations on March 17, 2025, while
modifying a summoning order against two accused persons. According to the prosecution, the
accused, Pawan and Akash, allegedly assaulted an 11-year-old girl, grabbing her breasts, breaking
her pyjama string, and trying to drag her beneath a culvert. However, they fled after passers-by
intervened.
The trial court charged them under Section 376 IPC (rape) and Section 18 POCSO (attempt). The
high court, however, reduced charges to Section 354-B IPC (assault with intent to disrobe) and
Sections 9/10 POCSO (aggravated sexual assault), stating there was no “determined intent” to
commit rape.
The SC later took suo motu cognizance of the order and stayed it on March 26, 2025. However, it
declined to frame any immediate guidelines itself, citing the need for a comprehensive study.
The SC has now directed the National Judicial Academy (NJA), Bhopal to form a committee of
experts to draft guidelines to inculcate "sensitivity and compassion" in judges and judicial
processes in cases of sexual offences.
The SC also stressed that the guidelines must be in simple, accessible language, avoiding complex
foreign expressions, and asked the NJA to submit its report preferably within three months.
Source: https://thefederal.com/category /news/sc-overturns-allahabad-hc-controversial-order-
child-assault-case-judicial-empathy-230406

content.passageText:
XIII. Under Indian law, vicarious liability in tort refers to a situation in which an employer is held
responsible for the tortious acts committed by his/her employees. The term “tort” refers to any civil
wrong that causes harm or injury to another person, and the term “vicarious liability” refers to the
legal responsibility that an employer has for the actions of his/her employees. The concept of
vicarious liability in tort is based on the principle of “respondeat superior” which means “let the
master answer” in Latin.
Vicarious liability in tort arises in specific relationships where one party (the employer or
principal) is held responsible for the tortious acts committed by another party (the employee or
agent). These relationships include:
Employer-Employee: Under the doctrine of vicarious liability, an employer can be held responsible
for the tortious acts of its employees. For example, if an employee of a company negligently causes
an accident while driving a company vehicle, the company may be held liable for any resulting
damages. This is because the employee was acting within the scope of their employment at the
time of the accident.
Principal-Agent: Similar to an employer-employee relationship, a principal can be held liable for
the tortious acts committed by their agent. An agent is someone who acts on behalf of the principal
and is authorized to do so. For example, if an agent of a real estate company commits fraud while
representing the company in a transaction, the company may be held liable for the agent’s actions.
In general, an employer is not held vicariously liable for the tortious acts committed by an
independent contractor. This is because an independent contractor is not an employee and is
generally considered to be operating as a separate business entity.
While vicarious liability in tort is a well-established legal doctrine, there are certain exceptions
where an employer or principal may not be held liable for the tortious acts committed by an
employee or agent. If an employee engages in an activity that is outside the scope of their
employment or agency, the employer may not be held liable for any resulting tortious acts. This is
known as the “frolic and detour” exception. For example, if an employee is tasked with making
deliveries for a company and, during the course of their duties, takes a personal detour to run
errands, any tortious acts committed during the detour may not be the responsibility of the
employer.
Generally, employers or principals are not held liable for intentional torts committed by their
employees or agents. This includes acts such as assault, battery, and defamation. However, if the
employer or principal knew or should have known about the employee’s propensity for such
behavior, they may still be held liable.
When an employee is borrowed or loaned to another employer, the borrowing employer may be
held liable for any tortious acts committed by the employee while under their control. This is
known as the “borrowed servant” rule. However, if the employee is under the control of their
original employer, that employer would still be held liable for any resulting tortious acts.
Source: https://lawbhoomi.com/vicarious-liability-in-tort/
content.questionText:
Ratan was a bus driver authorised by the bus owner, Farhan, to drive the bus. Once, Ratan
stepped out of the bus to get a cup of tea. In the meantime, Hasan, the conductor of the bus who
had never been authorised or trained to drive the bus, started driving it to move it out of the way
of traffic., during which he met with an accident. Which of the following correctly identifies the
liability arising from the accident?
options:
Ratan will be liable, as he was supposed to take reasonable care while parking the bus so that
it was out of the way of traffic.

Farhan will be liable, as he was the owner of the bus and Ratan was acting under his
authorisation.

Both Ratan and Farhan will be liable, as Farhan authorised Ratan, who in turn authorised
Hasan.
Only Hasan will be liable, as driving the bus was outside the course of his employment.
content.explanation: Hasan is the conductor. The passage bases vicarious liability on employees acting within the scope of employment.

content.questionText:
Suppose in the above question that when Ratan was stepping out of the bus, he asked Hasan to
park the bus nearby, even though he knew Hasan could not drive a bus properly. Hasan complied
with Ratan’s instructions and, while parking, met with an accident. Will Farhan be liable?
options:
No, only Ratan will be liable, as he negligently delegated his driving authority to Hasan
without proper authorization or consideration.

Yes, Farhan will be liable, as Hasan was acting as a conductor of the bus and was operating
within the scope of Farhan's authorized business operations.

Yes, Farhan will be liable, as Ratan was Farhan's employee who negligently delegated his
driving authority to Hasan within the scope of employment.

No, only Hasan will be liable, as driving the bus fell completely outside the scope of his
employment as a conductor and was not authorized.
content.explanation: Ratan negligently delegated driving to Hasan, but Hasan still acted within the employer’s operational sphere (parking the bus). Therefore, Farhan (employer) can still be vicariously liable through Ratan’s negligent delegation.

day, through whichever route is suitable. One day, while Bhola was picking up Chameli from the
hospital, the usual route had a lot of traffic. Therefore, he decided to take a longer route that he
did not usually take and met with an accident. Is Amit liable?
options: Yes, Amit is liable, as he was the owner of the car.

No, Amit is not liable, as Bhola was driving outside the course of his employment when the
accident occurred.
Yes, Amit is liable under the principle of vicarious liability.

content.passageText:
XIV. The Supreme Court of India recently expressed grave concern over an emerging and what it
termed an "alarming" trend of lawyers using artificial intelligence tools to draft court petitions
often without adequate verification. A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and
Justices B.V. Nagarathna and Joymalya Bagchi made these pointed remarks while hearing a
Public Interest Litigation (PIL) filed by academician Roop Rekha Verma, which sought the
framing of guidelines governing political speeches. Although the PIL itself pertained to a different
subject matter, the bench seized the opportunity to address a pressing concern that had been
surfacing repeatedly in court filings.
"We are alarmed to reflect that some lawyers have started using AI to draft petitions. It is
absolutely uncalled for," the Chief Justice observed, reflecting the judiciary's deepening unease.
Justice Nagarathna recalled encountering a fictitious citation, a case titled "Mercy vs Mankind"
that simply does not exist in any official law report or judicial record. The Chief Justice further
noted that a similar pattern had emerged before Justice Dipankar Datta, where not one but a
series of fabricated judgments had been cited in support of legal arguments, all of which were
found to be entirely non-existent.
The court also flagged a subtler but equally concerning problem: that even where cited judgments
were genuine, petitions sometimes contained fake quotations attributed to those verdicts. This

forces judges to spend additional time verifying the accuracy of each citation creating, as Justice
Nagarathna put it, "an additional burden on the part of the judges." Justice Bagchi added to these
concerns by lamenting the visible decline in the quality of legal drafting, particularly in special
leave petitions (SLPs). He observed that many such petitions are overloaded with lengthy extracts
from previous judgments, leaving little room for original legal reasoning or structured
argumentation a hallmark of skilled advocacy.
The Supreme Court clarified that it does not oppose the use of technology in legal practice
altogether. Indeed, the Court itself has embraced AI for translating judgments into Indian
languages and for case management through machine learning tools. However, it drew a firm line:
technology may assist with research, but it cannot replace the professional responsibility of an
advocate. Every citation, quotation, and legal proposition, the bench stressed, must be verified
against authentic, authorised sources before being placed on record. A lawyer, as an officer of the
court, carries a duty of diligence that no automated tool can discharge on their behalf. Blind
reliance on Al-generated content, the Court indicated, not only misleads the judiciary but strikes
at the very integrity of legal proceedings.
Source: https://www.thehindu.com/news /national /supreme-court-flags-the-risks-of-using-ai-for-
drafting-petitions/article70644488.ece

XV. The Supreme Court of India, on January 16, 2026, strongly criticised the growing and increasingly
common tendency among litigants to directly invoke Article 32 of the Constitution even in cases
where proceedings on the very same issue are already pending before a High Court. A bench
comprising Justice B.V. Nagarathna and Justice Ujjal Bhuyan took serious note of this practice
while hearing a writ petition filed under Article 32, despite the fact that an identical or
substantially similar plea was already under active consideration before the Bombay High Court.
The bench termed the petition a "gross misuse of the process of the court and of law" and
dismissed it without entertaining it on merits.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Expressing its displeasure in pointed terms, the bench observed that Article 32 was being invoked
with alarming frequency and for increasingly trivial reasons. The Court noted that litigants were
approaching the Supreme Court at even the slightest pretext — including the mere grant of an
adjournment in a High Court — rather than allowing those proceedings to reach their natural
conclusion. "Article 32 is being misused. The number of cases filed under Article 32 is
exponentially increasing. For everything, one adjournment, file Article 32 here. Especially those
surrounding Delhi are filing Article 82 petitions. What is this? It is a misuse," the bench
remarked, reflecting both frustration and constitutional concern.
Article 32 of the Constitution, which confers upon every citizen the fundamental right to approach
the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of their fundamental rights, is regarded as one of
the most important and cherished provisions in the constitutional framework. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
had famously described it as the "heart and soul of the Constitution." However, the apex court has
consistently held that this extraordinary remedy is not meant to be treated as a routine or first
resort. It is intended to be invoked only when there is a clear and demonstrated violation of
fundamental rights that warrants the direct intervention of the Supreme Court, and not as a
shortcut to bypass High Courts that are already seized of the same matter.
The Court reiterated that the appropriate constitutional remedy available before High Courts
under Article 226 — which confers a wide and expansive writ jurisdiction — must be exhausted or
at least genuinely engaged with, before a litigant seeks to invoke the Supreme Court's jurisdiction
under Article 32. By dismissing the petition, the bench sent a firm and unambiguous signal
against forum shopping and the casual erosion of the judicial hierarchy that such practices
inevitably bring about.

filed-despite-pending-high-court-case/

Article 32 protects the constitutional right to enforce fundamental rights, though this

content.passageText:
XV. The Supreme Court of India, on January 16, 2026, strongly criticised the growing and increasingly
common tendency among litigants to directly invoke Article 32 of the Constitution even in cases
where proceedings on the very same issue are already pending before a High Court. A bench
comprising Justice B.V. Nagarathna and Justice Ujjal Bhuyan took serious note of this practice
while hearing a writ petition filed under Article 32, despite the fact that an identical or
substantially similar plea was already under active consideration before the Bombay High Court.
The bench termed the petition a "gross misuse of the process of the court and of law" and
dismissed it without entertaining it on merits.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Expressing its displeasure in pointed terms, the bench observed that Article 32 was being invoked
with alarming frequency and for increasingly trivial reasons. The Court noted that litigants were
approaching the Supreme Court at even the slightest pretext — including the mere grant of an
adjournment in a High Court — rather than allowing those proceedings to reach their natural
conclusion. "Article 32 is being misused. The number of cases filed under Article 32 is
exponentially increasing. For everything, one adjournment, file Article 32 here. Especially those
surrounding Delhi are filing Article 82 petitions. What is this? It is a misuse," the bench
remarked, reflecting both frustration and constitutional concern.
Article 32 of the Constitution, which confers upon every citizen the fundamental right to approach
the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of their fundamental rights, is regarded as one of
the most important and cherished provisions in the constitutional framework. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
had famously described it as the "heart and soul of the Constitution." However, the apex court has
consistently held that this extraordinary remedy is not meant to be treated as a routine or first
resort. It is intended to be invoked only when there is a clear and demonstrated violation of
fundamental rights that warrants the direct intervention of the Supreme Court, and not as a
shortcut to bypass High Courts that are already seized of the same matter.
The Court reiterated that the appropriate constitutional remedy available before High Courts
under Article 226 — which confers a wide and expansive writ jurisdiction — must be exhausted or
at least genuinely engaged with, before a litigant seeks to invoke the Supreme Court's jurisdiction
under Article 32. By dismissing the petition, the bench sent a firm and unambiguous signal
against forum shopping and the casual erosion of the judicial hierarchy that such practices
inevitably bring about.

filed-despite-pending-high-court-case/

content.passageText:
XVI. “Deprivation (total loss) of personal liberty, which inter alia includes the right to eat or sleep when
one likes or to work or not to work as and when one pleases and several such rights sought to be
protected by the expression ‘personal liberty' in Article 21, is quite different from restriction
(which is only a partial control) of the right to move freely (which is relatively a minor right of a
citizen) as safeguarded by Article 19(1)(d). Deprivation of personal liberty has not the same
meaning as restriction of free movement in the territory of India. This is made clear when the
provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code in Chapter VIII relating to security of peace or
maintenance of public order are read. Therefore Article 19(5) cannot apply to a substantive law
depriving a citizen of personal liberty. I am unable to accept the contention that the word
‘deprivation’ includes within its scope 'restriction' when interpreting Article 21. Article 22
envisages the law of preventive detention. So does Article 246 read with Schedule Seven, List I,
Entry 9, and List III, Entry 3. Therefore, when the subject of preventive detention is specifically
dealt with in the Chapter on Fundamental Rights, I do not think it is proper to consider a
legislation permitting preventive detention as in conflict with the rights mentioned in Article
19(1). Article 19(1) does not purport to cover all aspects of liberty or of personal liberty. In that
article only certain phases of liberty are dealt with. www.lawpreptutorial.com
‘Personal liberty' would primarily mean liberty of the physical body. The rights given under Article
19(1) do not directly come under that description. They are rights which accompany the freedom or
liberty of the person. By their very nature they are freedoms of a person assumed to be in full
possession of his personal liberty. If Article 19 is considered to be the only article safeguarding
personal liberty, several well-recognised rights, as for instance, the right to eat or drink, the right
to work, play, swim and numerous other rights and activities and even the right to life will not be
deemed protected under the Constitution. I do not think that is the intention. It seems to me
improper to read Article 19 as dealing with the same subject as Article 21. Article 19 gives the
rights specified therein only to the citizens of India while Article 21 is applicable to all persons.
The word citizen is expressly defined in the Constitution to indicate only a certain section of the
inhabitants of India. Moreover, the protection given by Article 21 is very general. It is of '‘law'-
whatever that expression is interpreted to mean. The legislative restrictions on the law-making
powers of the legislature are not here prescribed in detail as in the case of the rights specified in
Article 19. In my opinion therefore Article 19 should be read as a separate complete article.”
Source: Kania CJ in AK Gopalan v. State of Madras 1950 AIR 27, 1950 SCR 88

facing in directions opposite to that of F. The one who wears a brown cap sits to the immediate

SECTION I
L	“Solitude and leadership—what can they possibly have to do with each other?” The question appears
paradoxical. Leadership is commonly imagined as a public performance: a figure at the head of an
army, a corporation, or a nation. Solitude, by contrast, evokes withdrawal—a man alone in the woods,
cut off from collective life. The essay challenges this contrast and argues that solitude is not the enemy
of leadership but its necessary precondition. Modern systems of education and _ professional
advancement, the author contends, prioritise success over judgment. Elite institutions excel at
producing individuals who can accumulate credentials, satisfy expectations, and follow established
paths. Such people are efficient and articulate, yet fundamentally unreflective. They can answer
questions posed by others but lack the capacity to frame their own. Achievement, divorced from
independent thought, results in authority without vision. Bureaucracy amplifies this failure. Drawing

content.passageText:
II.	Nancy’s trouble begins with a mistake so small it feels harmless: confusing one weekday for another.
She dismisses it as memory, not mind, expecting reassurance from her doctor. Instead, she finds herself
referred to a specialist who treats elderly patients, a development that unsettles her far more than the
error itself. What disturbs Nancy is not illness but the suspicion that something inside her is quietly
loosening.
Determined to retain control, she decides to locate the doctor’s office the evening before her
appointment. The choice reveals her fear of appearing confused or dependent. As she walks through the
town of Highman, the surroundings echo her inner unease. Shuttered shops, broken clocks, empty
streets, and misleading signs suggest a world that no longer operates by reliable markers. Nancy
recalls details vividly but forgets essentials—names, directions, and purposes. A scrap of paper meant
to guide her turns out to be meaningless.
Her wandering brings her to an unexpectedly beautiful garden, alive with flowers and fountains. Its
owner, a reserved man dressed in black, speaks to her with calm detachment. Their conversation feels
soothing, grounded in fragments of the past. When Nancy asks whether there once were “more sensible
explanations” for things, the question carries a personal weight rather than philosophical curiosity.
Acting on the man’s suggestion, Nancy drives to a rest home outside town. The building appears warm
and welcoming, but once inside, panic takes hold. Doors do not open. No one responds. Isolation presses
in, and fear overwhelms her.
The truth arrives quietly. A nurse addresses Nancy with familiarity. She is not visiting the home—she
belongs there. The journey through town was not a search for a doctor, but a return to memory. When
Nancy recalls her husband and her former independence, it becomes clear that what she has lost is not
direction, but time itself.
Source: Adapted from a literary short story exploring memory loss, ageing, and dementia

content.passageText:
II.	Nancy’s trouble begins with a mistake so small it feels harmless: confusing one weekday for another.
She dismisses it as memory, not mind, expecting reassurance from her doctor. Instead, she finds herself
referred to a specialist who treats elderly patients, a development that unsettles her far more than the
error itself. What disturbs Nancy is not illness but the suspicion that something inside her is quietly
loosening.
Determined to retain control, she decides to locate the doctor’s office the evening before her
appointment. The choice reveals her fear of appearing confused or dependent. As she walks through the
town of Highman, the surroundings echo her inner unease. Shuttered shops, broken clocks, empty
streets, and misleading signs suggest a world that no longer operates by reliable markers. Nancy
recalls details vividly but forgets essentials—names, directions, and purposes. A scrap of paper meant
to guide her turns out to be meaningless.
Her wandering brings her to an unexpectedly beautiful garden, alive with flowers and fountains. Its
owner, a reserved man dressed in black, speaks to her with calm detachment. Their conversation feels
soothing, grounded in fragments of the past. When Nancy asks whether there once were “more sensible
explanations” for things, the question carries a personal weight rather than philosophical curiosity.
Acting on the man’s suggestion, Nancy drives to a rest home outside town. The building appears warm
and welcoming, but once inside, panic takes hold. Doors do not open. No one responds. Isolation presses
in, and fear overwhelms her.
The truth arrives quietly. A nurse addresses Nancy with familiarity. She is not visiting the home—she
belongs there. The journey through town was not a search for a doctor, but a return to memory. When
Nancy recalls her husband and her former independence, it becomes clear that what she has lost is not
direction, but time itself.
Source: Adapted from a literary short story exploring memory loss, ageing, and dementia

content.passageText:
Til.	A night-time walk begins with irritation rather than reflection. Darkness feels hostile: the road is
uneven, streetlights are missing, and visibility is limited. The immediate response is to regard the dark
as unsafe and unnecessary, something modern life has worked to overcome. Light, by contrast, is
associated with order, progress, and control. Darkness appears to belong to an earlier stage of
development.
This perception does not remain unchanged. As the walk continues, the idea of an International Dark
Sky Park emerges—an area where artificial illumination is deliberately restricted. In such spaces, the
night sky is no longer obscured by human lighting. The Milky Way becomes clearly visible, sometimes
resembling early dawn. Darkness, once treated as absence, begins to register as presence.
Gradually, darkness is recast as preservation rather than deprivation. It allows room for wonder,
imagination, and perspective. Constant illumination, it is suggested, has reduced human sensitivity to
scale and mystery. When everything is visible, little feels significant; when nothing is concealed, depth
disappears. Darkness restores proportion by reminding humans of their limited place within a vast
universe.
The discussion extends beyond astronomy into ethical and psychological concerns. Darkness comes to
represent restraint—the decision not to dominate every environment or eliminate every uncertainty.
Just as natural systems depend on cycles of night to function, the human mind requires periods of
obscurity to reflect, imagine, and recalibrate.
Technology is not rejected, nor is a return to the past encouraged. Instead, balance is emphasised.
Protecting darkness is framed not as opposition to progress, but as a way of preserving a fragile human
capacity: the ability to experience awe without possession and beauty without explanation. Stepping
away from constant light is presented not as loss, but as an opportunity to recover perspective,
humility, and connection.
Source: Adapted from “Let There Be Dark” by Regan Penaluna, Nautilus, February 3, 2026.

content.passageText:
IV.	Byrnihat, an industrial town located on the Assam—Meghalaya border, has emerged as an example of
the environmental costs associated with rapid economic expansion. According to the IQAir World Air
Quality Report for 2024, published in March 2025, Byrnihat was ranked as the world’s most polluted
metropolitan area. The report recorded an annual average PM2.5 concentration of 128.2 micrograms
per cubic metre, a level significantly higher than the World Health Organization’s guideline of 5
micrograms per cubic metre.
Industrial activity is identified as the primary contributor to this condition. The town hosts around 80
operational factories, including cement plants, steel units, and distilleries. Industrial expansion has
proceeded at a rapid pace, with limited regulatory oversight. Byrnihat’s geographical location further
intensifies the problem. Situated in a valley surrounded by hills, the town experiences poor dispersion
of pollutants, causing emissions to accumulate rather than dissipate.
Daily life in the town unfolds alongside this industrial presence. Residential areas and recreational
spaces exist close to factory zones. Smoke from industrial units often reduces visibility, particularly in
the evenings. Pollution has become a constant feature rather than an occasional occurrence.
Health impacts have been increasingly reported. Medical practitioners and residents note a rise in
respiratory illnesses such as asthma and tuberculosis, along with an increase in cancer cases. These
conditions are linked to prolonged exposure to polluted air. Regulatory mechanisms appear ineffective.
Anti-pollution norms are frequently violated, and pollution control equipment in several factories is
reported to be non-functional. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Workers in cement factories face heightened risk due to regular inhalation of silica dust. Prolonged
exposure has led to cases of silicosis, a condition that often progresses into tuberculosis. Concerns have
also been raised about institutional oversight. Observers note that industrial permissions are granted
with limited assessment, and regulatory bodies lack autonomy. The situation reflects broader questions
about governance, regulation, and the balance between economic growth and public health.
Source: Anurab Dhar, “Poisoned by growth,” Frontline (The Hindu Group), Digital Exclusive photo
essay, January 23, 2026.

content.passageText:
V.	In the hospital ward, Leonard Thompson barely spoke. At fourteen, he had learned that effort was
expensive. When nurses asked how he felt, he answered with a shrug, conserving breath. His father
once tried optimism.
“Just a little longer,” he said. Leonard looked past him. He had heard that sentence before. The doctors
spoke quietly near the bed. “There isn’t much more we can do,” one of them said, not unkindly.
Diabetes, at the time, did not invite debate. It closed conversations. Then a different voice entered the
room. “We’d like to try something new,” Frederick Banting explained to Leonard’s parents. “It may not
work.”
Florence Thompson asked the only question that mattered. “And if we don’t try?”
Banting didn’t answer. He didn’t need to. The first injection did nothing. Leonard noticed the silence
that followed, heavier than before. No one said the word failure, but it hung in the air. He turned his
face to the wall. The familiar attitude returned: endure, expect nothing. Days later, another injection.
Then another. A nurse leaned closer and smiled. “You're brighter today,” she said.
Leonard frowned. “I feel... less tired,” he admitted, surprised by his own voice.
The change was slow but undeniable. “He asked for food,” a doctor noted, almost incredulous. “He sat
up.” Leonard himself tested the improvement cautiously, as if it might vanish if acknowledged too
quickly. When his father said, “You’re getting stronger,” Leonard replied, “Maybe,” but this time he
didn’t look away.
Elsewhere, confidence was hardening into belief. Banting, exhausted but alert, told a colleague, “It
works—but it has to work for everyone.” When asked about patents, he dismissed the idea. “Insulin
doesn’t belong to us. It belongs to the world.”

Years later, insulin would become routine, measured, refined, and mass-produced. But for Leonard, the
shift had already occurred. When a nurse asked him how he felt before discharge, he answered without
hesitation.
“Like I’m staying.” It was a small sentence. But in a world that once offered only delay, it marked a
decisive change—not just in treatment, but in attitude itself.
Source: Adapted from “The ‘miracle’ discovery that reversed the diabetes death sentence”,
NobelPrize.org, Nobel Prize Outreach (published November 138, 2024).

Union territory. There shall also be an option for self enumeration which shall be conducted in fifteen
days’ time period just before the start of house to (1) of thirty days,” RG&CCI Mritunjay Kumar
Narayan said in a gazette notification. This will be the first digital Census and the first to enumerate
caste in independent India.

enumerated during this phase. The pre-test or the preparatory exercise for the first phase of the
Census was held from November 10 to 30 last year in select areas across the country. It had sought
household responses to 35 questions, including the composition of the floor and roof of the house, main
cereal consumed, source of drinking water and cooking fuel, and the number of married couples in the
house.
